Several selected features may repeat the same information
Target scores remove all redundant columns automatically
The method always uses an exhaustive search
questions.explanation: Individual relevance does not tell us whether selected features are mutually redundant.

questions.question: What would a simple variance-threshold filter likely remove?
choices: A feature whose value is almost constant
A feature with several useful levels
The target variable
Every numerical feature
questions.explanation: A nearly constant feature has little observed variation and may fall below a chosen variance threshold.

questions.question: Two selected features are highly correlated with each other. What should you investigate?
choices: Whether both are necessarily causal
Whether one must be categorical
Whether their information is redundant
Whether the target can be removed
questions.explanation: A high inter-feature correlation can indicate overlapping information even when both features relate to the target.

questions.question: For a numerical feature and numerical target, which simple association score could be used?
choices: A category-count pie chart
Only the file size
Only a ZIP-code mapping
Pearson or Spearman correlation
questions.explanation: The lecture lists correlation coefficients for numerical input versus numerical target relationships.

questions.question: In a chi-square independence test, what is compared?
choices: The numerical mean before and after scaling
Observed category counts and counts expected under independence
Training accuracy and a map legend
The same category name in two files
questions.explanation: The test contrasts observed contingency-table counts with expected counts if the variables were independent.

questions.question: If observed category counts differ greatly from counts expected under independence, what does that suggest?
choices: Evidence of an association with the target
Proof the variables are independent
The feature must be constant
The outcome is necessarily caused by the feature
questions.explanation: Large observed-versus-expected differences give evidence against independence, not proof of causation.

questions.question: Which chi-square feature would usually be preferred when selecting for association?
choices: The one with the smallest test statistic and largest p-value
The one with perfectly matching observed and expected counts
The one with a larger test statistic and smaller p-value
The one with the longest category labels
questions.explanation: The slide says to choose features with higher chi-square statistics or lower p-values, indicating stronger evidence against independence.

questions.question: What does entropy describe?
choices: Expected uncertainty in a variable
The number of columns in a table
The average numerical feature value
The amount of feature scaling
questions.explanation: Entropy quantifies how uncertain a variable is before its outcome is known.

questions.question: Which binary event has higher entropy: a 50/50 split or a 90/10 split?
choices: The 90/10 split
Both necessarily have zero entropy
The 50/50 split
Entropy cannot be compared for binary events
questions.explanation: A balanced binary outcome is harder to predict in advance and therefore has higher entropy.

questions.question: What does conditional entropy H(target | feature) mean?
choices: The count of missing target values
The uncertainty remaining in the target after knowing the feature
The target mean before seeing any data
The correlation between two features
questions.explanation: Conditional entropy asks how uncertain the target remains when the feature value is known.

questions.question: Which expression gives the mutual information between a target Y and feature X?
choices: H(Y) + H(Y | X)
H(Y | X) - H(Y)
H(X) multiplied by H(Y)
H(Y) - H(Y | X)
questions.explanation: Mutual information is the uncertainty in Y removed by knowing X.

questions.question: A feature cuts target uncertainty from 1 bit to 0.2 bits. What is its mutual information with the target?
choices: 0.8 bits
1.2 bits
-0.8 bits
0.2 bits
questions.explanation: MI is original entropy minus remaining conditional entropy: 1 - 0.2 = 0.8 bits.

questions.question: Which feature has higher mutual information with the target?
choices: The one leaving more uncertainty after it is known
The one removing more uncertainty about the target
The one with the longest name
The one with the largest raw numerical values
questions.explanation: Higher MI means a feature removes more target uncertainty; lower remaining uncertainty is better.

questions.question: If a feature and target are independent, what is their theoretical mutual information?
choices: Always negative
Exactly their joint entropy
One by definition
Zero
questions.explanation: Knowing an independent feature does not reduce uncertainty in the target.

questions.question: Can theoretical mutual information be negative?
choices: No; it measures a nonnegative reduction in uncertainty
Yes, whenever Pearson correlation is negative
Yes, for a 90/10 target
Only when the data is categorical
questions.explanation: MI is nonnegative in theory; independence gives zero, not a negative value.

questions.question: Why might mutual information find a useful feature that Pearson correlation misses?
choices: MI ignores the target
Pearson tests categorical names only
MI can detect nonlinear dependence, while Pearson measures linear association
MI requires a perfect straight line
questions.explanation: The slide states that information can be shared through any dependence, including nonlinear patterns.

questions.question: How can mutual information scores be used for a simple feature-selection filter?
choices: Choose only features with the lowest possible score
Replace every value with its MI score
Use the score to prove causation
Rank features and keep the top K
questions.explanation: The lecture proposes scoring all features by MI and selecting the highest-ranked K.

questions.question: What does mRMR stand for?
choices: Maximum rows, minimum regression
Minimum relevance, maximum redundancy
Minimum redundancy, maximum relevance
Maximum residual, minimum range
questions.explanation: The aim is useful target information with as little repeated information among selected features as possible.

questions.question: In mRMR, what does relevance measure?
choices: A candidate feature's relationship with the target
The candidate's relationship with a chart title
The number of rows in the dataset
The similarity among already selected features only
questions.explanation: Relevance is how much information a candidate feature provides about the target.

questions.question: In mRMR, what does redundancy measure?
choices: Only the feature's relation to the target
The percentage of missing rows
How large the feature's numbers are
How much the candidate overlaps with features already selected
questions.explanation: Redundancy compares a candidate with the current selected subset, looking for repeated information.

questions.question: Why is the first mRMR feature chosen by maximum relevance alone?
choices: The target is not yet known
No feature has been selected yet, so there is no selected-set redundancy to assess
All features have identical redundancy
The first feature is always alphabetical
questions.explanation: Before the first selection, the selected subset is empty, so only relevance to the target can guide the choice.

questions.question: After one feature is selected, what does mRMR consider for each candidate?
choices: Relevance to target together with redundancy against the selected subset
Only the candidate's spelling
Only the selected feature's variance
Whether the candidate was first in the file
questions.explanation: The iterative score balances useful target association against information already supplied by selected features.

questions.question: Litres is already selected. Gallons predicts the target well but is simply litres in another unit. How might mRMR treat gallons?
choices: Always select it because relevance is the only score
Treat it as irrelevant to the target
Penalise it for high redundancy with litres
Convert it to a date feature
questions.explanation: Gallons can be relevant yet add little new information after the equivalent litres feature is included.

questions.question: Which expression matches a common mRMR score?
choices: Relevance plus redundancy
Redundancy minus relevance
Feature count multiplied by target mean
Relevance minus redundancy
questions.explanation: One common mRMR form rewards target relevance while subtracting overlap with selected features.

questions.question: How does an iterative mRMR feature subset grow?
choices: By deleting all features at once
By adding one best-scoring feature at a time until K are selected
By keeping only the first two columns
By creating a new target at every step
questions.explanation: The procedure iteratively adds the candidate with the best relevance-versus-redundancy score.

questions.question: When do embedded methods carry out feature selection?
choices: Only after every possible subset is tested
During model training
Before any data is observed
Only after deployment
questions.explanation: Selection is built into the learner's fitting process rather than a separate repeated subset search.

questions.question: Why are embedded methods often faster than wrappers?
choices: They never fit any model
They always use only two features
They never evaluate data
They do not need a separate model fit for every candidate subset
questions.explanation: Embedded selection occurs as part of training, avoiding many wrapper-style retraining rounds.

questions.question: Which criteria can be used to choose a decision-tree split?
choices: Information gain or Gini impurity
Only the feature name
Only the largest raw number
The order of rows in the CSV
questions.explanation: Tree nodes choose a useful split using a metric such as information gain or Gini impurity.

questions.question: What does bootstrap sampling 'with replacement' mean for one random-forest tree?
choices: Every original row appears exactly once
Only features, never rows, are sampled
A row may be drawn more than once while another row is not drawn
The tree uses only rows with missing values
questions.explanation: After each draw the row remains eligible, so duplicates and omissions can occur in the bootstrap sample.

questions.question: In a random forest, what is typically restricted at each split?
choices: The target must become numerical
A random subset of candidate features is considered
The number of rows must equal one
The split must use the same feature in every tree
questions.explanation: Each node considers a random subset of features, helping the trees differ from one another.

questions.question: What does the forest aggregate across its trees?
choices: Only column names
Only the raw target values
Only one chosen root split
Tree predictions and feature-importance scores
questions.explanation: The slide describes combining tree predictions and averaging feature importances across the ensemble.

questions.question: How is a random-forest classification prediction commonly combined?
choices: By majority vote among tree predictions
By deleting every tree except the first
By always taking the largest feature value
By comparing only the chart colours
questions.explanation: For classification, the ensemble commonly votes across the trees; regression can average predictions.

questions.question: What kind of coefficient penalty does LASSO use?
choices: No penalty at all
Only a penalty on the number of rows
An L1 penalty on absolute coefficient values
An L2 penalty only
questions.explanation: LASSO adds an absolute-value (L1) penalty to the fitting objective.

questions.question: How does LASSO's L1 penalty enable feature selection?
choices: It creates more one-hot columns
It can drive some feature coefficients exactly to zero
It copies the target into each feature
It guarantees every feature has equal weight
questions.explanation: A zero coefficient removes that feature's contribution to the fitted linear model.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes L1 from L2 regularisation for feature selection?
choices: L1 and L2 both force every coefficient to zero
L2 selects exactly one feature
L1 has no effect on coefficients
L1 can create exact zeros; L2 usually shrinks toward zero without exact zeros
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts LASSO's sparse L1 solution with L2's shrinkage toward zero.

questions.question: A fitted LASSO model gives one feature a coefficient of exactly zero. What does that imply for this fitted model?
choices: The feature contributes nothing to its linear prediction
The feature has no possible use in any other model
The feature proves the target is random
The feature must contain missing values
questions.explanation: A zero coefficient excludes that feature from this model's prediction, not necessarily from every possible model.

questions.question: What is varied across k-fold cross-validation folds when checking a feature set's stability?
choices: The names of all features
The definition of the target
The row splits used for training and validation
The meaning of the score
questions.explanation: K-fold cross-validation partitions observations into different training and validation row sets to test generalisation.

questions.question: Why evaluate a selected feature set over multiple folds?
choices: To check whether its performance holds up across different row splits
To guarantee it is the only useful feature set
To convert every column to a date
To avoid ever training a model
questions.explanation: A stable feature set should perform reasonably consistently beyond one fortunate train/validation split.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes k-fold CV from changing feature subsets?
choices: K-fold means using K different target definitions
K-fold creates new raw features automatically
K-fold requires a different feature name in every fold
K-fold changes training/validation rows; a selector may be evaluated within those folds
questions.explanation: CV splits observations, while selection chooses columns; the two procedures can be combined.

questions.question: What is one way to combine several feature selectors?
choices: Ignore every selector except the first
Count how often each feature is chosen, or use weighted votes
Rename all features to the same label
Always select every available feature
questions.explanation: The slide suggests aggregating selectors by selection frequency or weighted voting.

questions.question: A feature is chosen by 8 of 10 selectors. What does selection frequency describe?
choices: How many times a model was deployed
The number of missing rows
How consistently selectors chose that feature
Its exact causal effect
questions.explanation: Selection frequency summarises agreement among selectors; it is not proof of causality.

questions.question: Is one feature-selection method best for every dataset?
choices: No; the suitable method depends on the data and problem
Yes; exhaustive search is always best
Yes; variance threshold is always enough
Yes; LASSO always wins
questions.explanation: The conclusion explicitly says there is no universally best feature-selection method.

questions.question: How can domain knowledge help choose features?
choices: By replacing all validation
By proving a feature is causal
By guaranteeing a normal distribution
By identifying features that are meaningful, plausible, and available for the task
questions.explanation: An expert can judge whether a feature makes sense for the real problem and can actually be used.

questions.question: What is a sensible practical approach to feature selection?
choices: Pick one selector once and never revisit it
Iterate over suitable methods and cross-validate the resulting feature set
Use every column regardless of meaning
Choose features solely by alphabetic order
questions.explanation: Selection may take several iterations, and the chosen set should be checked by cross-validation.

questions.question: As a reminder, what is possible when a random-forest tree takes a bootstrap sample with replacement?
choices: Every row must appear exactly once
No row may be repeated
Some rows repeat and some original rows are omitted
Only features are sampled, never observations
questions.explanation: Sampling with replacement keeps every row eligible after each draw, allowing repeats and leaving some rows out.

questions.question: What does SelectFromModel use to choose features?
choices: Only the order of columns
A chosen fitted learning model and its selection settings
A handwritten list of every row
Only the colour of a chart
questions.explanation: The slide describes giving SelectFromModel a learning algorithm and parameters so it can select features from the fitted model.

questions.question: Which property makes a sequence a time series rather than an unordered set of rows?
choices: It contains only numerical values
It has no missing values
The temporal order of observations matters
Every observation is independent
questions.explanation: A time series is a set of observations ordered by time; their sequence carries information.

questions.question: Which statement about neighbouring time-series observations is most accurate?
choices: They are often related, but not guaranteed to be correlated
They are always identical
They must be perfectly predictable
Their order may always be shuffled safely
questions.explanation: Adjacent observations often have dependence, but it is not a universal guarantee.

questions.question: Why can randomly shuffling a time series before exploration be misleading?
choices: It makes every value negative
It converts dates to categories
It proves the series stationary
It destroys the original temporal sequence and lag relationships
questions.explanation: Shuffling breaks the order needed to inspect trends, timing, and possible dependence across lags.

questions.question: Why must an ambiguous date such as 03/04/2026 be interpreted with its source format?
choices: Because every date uses UTC
It could mean 3 April or 4 March
Because all dates are Unix timestamps
Because dates have no order
questions.explanation: Day-first and month-first formats can assign different calendar dates to the same string.

questions.question: What do Unix epoch timestamps represent?
choices: A time offset measured from an agreed epoch, commonly 1 January 1970
A category rank
The number of rows in a dataset
A moving-average window size
questions.explanation: An epoch timestamp counts elapsed time since a fixed origin; the unit, such as seconds or milliseconds, must also be checked.

questions.question: Two sensors record the same event in different time zones. What should you do before aligning their timestamps?
choices: Sort each file by its row number only
Drop all observations from one sensor
Convert times to a common time basis such as UTC
Assume clock times refer to the same instant
questions.explanation: A common time basis avoids matching different instants that happen to have the same local clock display.

questions.question: What is a possible consequence of ignoring daylight-saving changes in timestamped data?
choices: All numerical values become zero
Events may be aligned to the wrong hour
The data becomes categorical
Every timestamp becomes missing
questions.explanation: Local clock offsets can change over time, so time-zone handling matters when comparing events.

questions.question: Before plotting or joining two time-series datasets, which alignment check matters?
choices: Only whether the files have the same name
Only whether the y-axis is colourful
Only whether both datasets have a median
Whether time zones, periods, and sampling frequencies are compatible
questions.explanation: Comparisons can be misleading if timestamps or frequencies refer to different periods or instants.

questions.question: What does sampling frequency describe?
choices: The number of categories in a feature
How often observations are recorded in time
How many models are trained
The strength of Pearson correlation
questions.explanation: Frequency expresses observation rate, such as readings per second or one reading per day.

questions.question: Readings arrive at 09:00, 09:01, 09:07, and 09:08. What should you check?
choices: Whether the six-minute gap means irregular sampling or missing periods
Whether every value is Gaussian
Whether the records should be alphabetised
Whether all readings are outliers
questions.explanation: The timestamp differences are not evenly spaced; the gap may matter for analysis and resampling.

questions.question: What is upsampling a time series?
choices: Moving to fewer observations per unit time
Randomly shuffling the observations
Moving to a higher observation frequency
Replacing time with a category label
questions.explanation: Upsampling creates a finer time grid, such as moving from hourly to minute-level positions.

questions.question: After upsampling hourly observations to a minute-by-minute grid, what usually needs attention?
choices: Every original row must be deleted
A random target must be added
The original readings must be duplicated as real measurements
New time slots have no observed value and need a justified fill or interpolation
questions.explanation: A finer grid does not create new measurements; inserted gaps require an explicit handling choice.

questions.question: How is downsampling from minute readings to hourly readings commonly performed?
choices: By inventing sixty new values
By grouping each hour and aggregating its readings
By changing the date format only
By swapping the training target
questions.explanation: Downsampling reduces frequency and requires an aggregation rule such as mean or sum.

questions.question: You downsample fuel sales into daily totals. Which aggregation is appropriate for total sales per day?
choices: The first sale only
The mean without considering the task
The sum of sales within each day
A forward-filled value from the previous day
questions.explanation: Daily totals require adding the sales in each day's time bin; another question might call for a mean instead.

questions.question: What does 1 Hz sampling mean?
choices: One reading per second
One reading per minute
Fifteen readings per second
One reading per year
questions.explanation: Hertz counts observations per second, so 1 Hz is one sample each second.

questions.question: GPS readings are at 1 Hz while accelerometer readings are at 15 Hz. Which sensor has finer original time resolution?
choices: GPS, because 1 is lower
Both are identical
Neither has timestamps
The accelerometer
questions.explanation: Fifteen samples per second can capture faster changes than one sample per second.

questions.question: Why might downsampling 15 Hz acceleration data to 1 Hz be risky when studying sudden motion?
choices: It guarantees all samples are duplicated
Rapid changes may be averaged away
It increases the original resolution
It removes the time zone automatically
questions.explanation: Short acceleration spikes can disappear when many high-frequency readings are compressed into one low-frequency value.

questions.question: A fuel-transaction table has no row for Tuesday because nobody refuelled. Is that necessarily a missing sensor reading?
choices: Yes, every date must have a transaction
Yes, unless Tuesday was a holiday
No; no event occurred, which differs from a failed scheduled measurement
No, because dates cannot be missing
questions.explanation: Event-based data may have no record when nothing happened; scheduled sensor data may have a missing reading when a sample was expected.

questions.question: A sensor is expected to report every minute but has no reading at 12:03. What should you investigate?
choices: Whether the scheduled measurement is missing and how much can change during the gap
Whether the sensor name is alphabetical
Whether a transaction occurred at 12:03
Whether all nearby readings are identical
questions.explanation: A gap in an expected fixed-frequency stream may hide important movement or fluctuations.

questions.question: What is a rolling window of length four readings?
choices: Four unrelated columns
The entire dataset shuffled four times
Exactly four future values only
The current reading together with the three preceding readings
questions.explanation: A four-reading lookback window uses the four most recent observations available at that point.

questions.question: A three-reading simple moving average sees the sequence 2, 4, 9. What is the first full-window average?
questions.explanation: The first complete three-reading window has mean (2 + 4 + 9) / 3 = 5.

questions.question: For a full-window simple moving average of length X, how many initial positions lack a complete window?
choices: Exactly one for every X
None
questions.explanation: The first X - 1 positions do not yet have X observations behind them, so the full-window average is undefined there.

questions.question: What is the usual effect of a simple moving average on a noisy series?
choices: It guarantees all sudden spikes are preserved
It makes the observations independent
It smooths short-term fluctuations
It proves a causal trend
questions.explanation: A moving average combines nearby readings, reducing rapid variation while potentially hiding brief events.

questions.question: How does an exponentially weighted moving average differ from an equal-weight simple moving average?
choices: It ignores every recent observation
It always uses future observations
It replaces time with category labels
It places more weight on recent readings
questions.explanation: Exponential weighting decreases the influence of older observations instead of treating all readings in a fixed window equally.

questions.question: Which statement about filling a short time-series gap is most accurate?
choices: Linear interpolation is always safe regardless of the pattern
The chosen fill method should reflect whether values change smoothly or fluctuate sharply
Every gap should be filled with zero
Forward filling creates a new measured value
questions.explanation: Interpolation is an estimate, not an observation; a rapid or seasonal process needs extra care.

questions.question: Why can straight-line interpolation through a strongly seasonal gap be misleading?
choices: It may ignore the recurring rise-and-fall pattern inside the gap
It always raises every value
It changes every timestamp to UTC
It proves the seasonality is random
questions.explanation: A straight line may miss seasonal structure; the slide suggests accounting for seasonality when imputing such gaps.

questions.question: Which description best captures weak stationarity in a time series?
choices: Every value must be identical
The mean, variance, and lag-dependent covariance stay stable over time
The series must increase every day
The observations must be independent
questions.explanation: Stationarity concerns stable underlying statistical properties, not a perfectly flat sequence of values.

questions.question: A stationary time series has different readings from one day to the next. Is that possible?
choices: No, every reading must equal the mean
No, its variance must be zero
Only if there is no timestamp
Yes, readings can fluctuate while the generating properties remain stable
questions.explanation: Values can vary around a stable process; stationarity does not require constant observed values.

questions.question: A series has a persistent upward trend in its level. How should you usually regard the raw series?
choices: Non-stationary as-is because its mean level changes with time
Stationary because values rise steadily
Stationary because its timestamps are ordered
Impossible to plot
questions.explanation: A time-varying mean conflicts with ordinary weak stationarity, though removing a deterministic trend may help.

questions.question: In an autoregressive AR(1) expression y(t) = alpha × y(t-1) + error(t), what is used to help predict the current value?
choices: Only the date label
An unrelated variable's future value
A past value of the same series plus an error term
Only a category count
questions.explanation: An autoregression relates the series to its own lagged value, with an innovation or error term.

questions.question: What happens in the simple AR(1) example when alpha equals 1?
choices: All observations become zero
Shocks accumulate in a unit-root, random-walk-like process
The process becomes perfectly seasonal
Every shock disappears after one step
questions.explanation: With alpha = 1, each new value carries the previous value plus a shock; accumulated shocks can make variance grow over time.

questions.question: What is the null hypothesis of the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test?
choices: The series has zero variance
The series is certainly Gaussian
The target is independent of every feature
A unit root is present, implying non-stationarity in this test
questions.explanation: ADF starts from the unit-root hypothesis; evidence against it supports rejecting that non-stationary null.

questions.question: An ADF test returns p = 0.01 at a 5% threshold. What is the usual conclusion?
choices: Reject the unit-root null; evidence favours stationarity under the tested specification
Accept the unit-root null as proven
The series must have no noise
The test cannot be interpreted because p is below 0.05
questions.explanation: A sufficiently small p-value provides evidence against the ADF null of a unit root.

questions.question: At 5% significance, an ADF test gives p = 0.42. What should you say?
choices: The series is proven stationary
The unit-root null has been rejected
There is insufficient evidence to reject the unit-root null
All future values are perfectly predictable
questions.explanation: A large p-value does not reject the ADF unit-root null; it does not prove the null is true.

questions.question: What is the null hypothesis of a KPSS test configured for trend stationarity?
choices: The series has a unit root
The series is stationary around a deterministic trend
The series has no timestamps
The series is independent of every feature
questions.explanation: Unlike ADF, this KPSS version begins with trend stationarity as its null hypothesis.

questions.question: A KPSS test for trend stationarity gives a very small p-value. Which interpretation is appropriate?
choices: It proves a perfectly constant series
It confirms the stationary null
It is interpreted exactly like an ADF small p-value
It is evidence against the trend-stationary null
questions.explanation: A small KPSS p-value leads you to reject its stationarity null, opposite to the ADF null direction.

questions.question: Which pairing of test and null hypothesis is correct?
choices: ADF: unit root; KPSS: stationarity under its chosen level/trend specification
ADF: stationarity; KPSS: unit root
Both: no missing values
Both: perfect prediction
questions.explanation: The two tests start from different null hypotheses, so their p-values must not be read as though the nulls match.

questions.question: For the ADF decision rule shown in the lecture, what supports rejecting a unit root at 5%?
choices: Only a large p-value
Only a positive time trend
A p-value below 0.05 and a test statistic more negative than the 5% critical value
Exactly equal readings at all times
questions.explanation: The lecture combines a small p-value with a test statistic below the chosen critical cutoff when interpreting ADF.

questions.question: Why is stationarity useful for many time-series methods?
choices: It makes all observations independent
It gives a more stable underlying pattern for analysis and meets assumptions of many methods
It removes every outlier automatically
It guarantees exact future predictions
questions.explanation: Stable process properties make modelling and interpretation easier, and many tools assume stationarity.

questions.question: Which statement is FALSE?
choices: A stationary series may fluctuate from one timestamp to another
A persistent changing mean can indicate non-stationarity
An AR model can use a series' own past values
Stationarity means every observed value must stay exactly the same
questions.explanation: Stationarity means stable statistical properties, not identical observations at every time point.

questions.question: What is a first difference at time t?
choices: The original level y(t)
The previous level divided by the current level
The current level minus the previous level
The mean of all future levels
questions.explanation: First differencing calculates y(t) - y(t-1), expressing change between adjacent observations.

questions.question: A series has levels 10, 13, 18. What are its first differences?
choices: 3 and 5
10 and 13
13 and 18
-3 and -5
questions.explanation: The differences are 13 - 10 = 3 and 18 - 13 = 5.

questions.question: After first differencing, what do the new values mainly represent?
choices: The original absolute levels
The exact seasonal period
The number of categories
Changes from one observation to the next
questions.explanation: Differencing replaces levels with adjacent changes, which may help remove a persistent level trend.

questions.question: Why might differencing be applied to a series with a rising level trend?
choices: To turn dates into text labels
To focus on changes and potentially reduce the trend's non-stationarity
To guarantee the values become independent
To prove the series is multiplicative
questions.explanation: Successive differences can remove or reduce a trend in the level, though the resulting series still needs checking.

questions.question: Which transformations are mentioned as ways to change a non-stationary series' scale or variance?
choices: Only row shuffling
Only one-hot encoding
Log, square-root, or power transformations
Replacing all values with the median
questions.explanation: The slide lists log, square-root, and power transformations among approaches toward stationarity.

questions.question: A positive-valued series has swings that grow as its level rises. Why might a log transform help?
choices: It can compress larger values and make spread more stable
It removes every seasonal event automatically
It creates additional measurements
It guarantees stationarity without testing
questions.explanation: Logging positive values compresses large magnitudes and may stabilise growth in variation.

questions.question: What must you check before taking an ordinary logarithm of observed series values?
choices: Whether every timestamp has the same weekday
Whether the series has exactly one category
Whether all levels are equal
Whether the input values are positive or need a justified adjustment
questions.explanation: The ordinary real-valued log is undefined for zero or negative inputs, so those values need a deliberate treatment.

questions.question: After differencing or transforming a series, what should be done before treating it as stationary?
choices: Assume the transformation worked
Reinspect and test the transformed series
Shuffle its timestamps
Always remove every seasonal component
questions.explanation: A transformation may help but does not guarantee stationarity; the new series needs another check.

questions.question: Which set names the usual components used to decompose a time series?
choices: Mean, median, mode
Latitude, longitude, altitude
Trend, seasonality, and noise
Rows, columns, labels
questions.explanation: Decomposition separates longer-term movement, fixed-period patterns, and irregular residual variation.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes seasonality from a broader cycle?
choices: Seasonality repeats at fixed intervals; cycles need not have a fixed period
Cycles are always random noise
Seasonality never repeats
Both must occur every day
questions.explanation: A seasonal pattern has a regular clock or calendar period, while a cycle can recur without exact timing.

questions.question: Seasonal swings stay about 20 units above and below the trend even as the level rises. Which decomposition form is a reasonable first guess?
choices: Multiplicative, because swings scale with the level
Additive, because the absolute seasonal amplitude stays similar
Random walk, because all values are equal
No decomposition can represent seasonality
questions.explanation: A roughly constant absolute seasonal effect fits an additive trend + seasonal + noise view.

questions.question: Seasonal swings grow in proportion to the series' rising level. Which decomposition form is a reasonable first guess?
choices: Additive, because seasonal size never changes
Noisy, because a seasonal pattern cannot grow
Multiplicative, because the seasonal effect scales with the level
Differenced, because every value must be zero
questions.explanation: Proportional growth in seasonal amplitude points toward a multiplicative structure.

questions.question: Which component describes irregular variation not explained by trend or seasonality?
choices: A fixed calendar season
The timestamp index
The long-term trend
Noise or residual variation
questions.explanation: Noise is the irregular remainder after the more systematic components are accounted for.

questions.question: Daily values rise and fall, but their overall level slowly increases over years. What is the long-term component?
choices: A fixed daily season
A trend
A missing observation
A category label
questions.explanation: Trend captures the longer-term direction even when individual observations fluctuate.

questions.question: Why use a moving average while exploring a noisy series?
choices: To guarantee all spikes are preserved
To remove the time axis
To make every reading identical
To smooth short-term fluctuations and reveal longer-term movement
questions.explanation: Averaging neighbouring observations can make an underlying trend easier to see.

questions.question: What is a likely problem with a moving-average window that is too short for a noisy series?
choices: Much of the short-term noise remains
Every seasonal effect disappears
No observations retain timestamps
The average necessarily becomes negative
questions.explanation: A short window smooths less, so rapid fluctuations can still obscure the larger pattern.

questions.question: What is a likely problem with a moving-average window that is too long?
choices: It guarantees overfitting
It creates new high-frequency readings
It can smooth away meaningful changes
It becomes a categorical feature
questions.explanation: Excessive smoothing can lose useful local information.

questions.question: A monthly series has a roughly yearly seasonal cycle. Which moving-average window is a sensible starting point for estimating its trend?
choices: Exactly one minute
Around 12 months, then inspect the result
The entire dataset regardless of length
One observation only
questions.explanation: A window near the seasonal length is a useful starting guess, but window choice remains iterative.

questions.question: Why might trend-window selection require several attempts?
choices: A moving average changes the original timestamp order
All datasets have the same season length
The target variable must be deleted
The true seasonal length and the right amount of smoothing may not be known in advance
questions.explanation: Different windows reveal or suppress different patterns, so inspect and adjust rather than assuming one universal size.

questions.question: In an additive decomposition y = trend + seasonality + noise, how do you detrend y?
choices: Subtract the estimated trend from y
Divide the trend by y
Multiply y by the trend
Randomly shuffle y
questions.explanation: Subtracting trend leaves the additive remainder of seasonality plus noise.

questions.question: In a multiplicative decomposition y = trend × seasonality × noise, how do you detrend y when trend is nonzero?
choices: Subtract y from the trend
Add the trend to y
Divide y by the estimated trend
Set every value to one
questions.explanation: Dividing by trend leaves the multiplicative remainder of seasonality times noise.

questions.question: After removing an estimated trend, what can still remain in the series?
choices: Only a constant zero
Seasonality and noise
Only the original trend
No time dependence by definition
questions.explanation: Detrending removes one component; periodic and irregular variation may remain.

questions.question: What should you do after removing a trend to see whether the result is suitable for stationary modelling?
choices: Assume the remainder must be stationary
Ignore any remaining seasonal pattern
Replace all observations with their mean
Inspect the remainder and check stationarity again
questions.explanation: Removing trend may help but does not guarantee stationarity, especially when seasonality remains.

questions.question: Which description best fits seasonality?
choices: An irregular event that never repeats
A change in measurement units
A repeating pattern at a fixed, predictable time interval
Any single extreme observation
questions.explanation: Seasonality follows a regular time period, such as day of week or month of year.

questions.question: What makes a longer economic boom-and-bust cycle different from fixed-period seasonality?
choices: Its recurrence need not follow one fixed time interval
It must occur every Monday
It has no possible effect on a trend
It can never recur
questions.explanation: Cycles can recur, but their duration is not predictably fixed like a seasonal period.

questions.question: In daily data, autocorrelation peaks at lags 7, 14, and 21. What pattern does this suggest?
choices: A three-hour cycle
No temporal structure
A yearly pattern
A weekly repeating pattern
questions.explanation: Daily observations separated by multiples of seven days are similar, indicating weekly repetition.

questions.question: A monthly series has an autocorrelation peak at lag 12. Which period is suggested?
choices: Twelve days
About one year
Twelve hours
No repeating period
questions.explanation: Twelve monthly observations separate values by roughly a year.

questions.question: In autocorrelation, what does a lag of seven identify?
choices: A correlation magnitude of 7
Exactly seven missing observations
Separation by seven observation intervals
Seven different features
questions.explanation: Lag indicates temporal separation; the correlation coefficient supplies the strength and direction.

questions.question: What does autocorrelation compare?
choices: A series with lagged versions of itself
Two unrelated category names
Only the smallest and largest value
The filename and timestamp
questions.explanation: Autocorrelation measures similarity between observations of the same series at different time lags.

questions.question: A detrended monthly series has a clear January effect. How could that seasonal effect be estimated?
choices: Use only one January value and discard the rest
Ignore the calendar month
Replace all months with the yearly total
Average the values for each calendar month across years
questions.explanation: Repeated positions within the seasonal cycle can be averaged to estimate a typical effect for each month.

questions.question: Under additive decomposition y = trend + seasonality + noise, what remains after subtracting trend and seasonality?
choices: The original trend
A residual intended to contain mainly noise
Only a new seasonal signal
A guaranteed zero at every time
questions.explanation: The additive residual is y - trend - seasonality; it ideally contains the unexplained variation.

questions.question: Under multiplicative decomposition y = trend × seasonality × noise, how do you isolate the residual when the components are nonzero?
choices: Add trend and seasonality to y
Subtract trend only
Divide y by the product of trend and seasonality
Shuffle the observations
questions.explanation: Dividing y by trend × seasonality leaves the multiplicative residual factor.

questions.question: After removing estimated trend and seasonality, which test is still important?
choices: Check whether the residual is stationary
Assume the residual is stationary automatically
Check whether all values are identical
Convert the residual to category labels
questions.explanation: Decomposition is not proof of stationarity; the residual should be inspected and tested.

questions.question: How can you assess whether an additive or multiplicative decomposition is plausible?
choices: Look only at the file extension
Assume both are always identical
Ignore the original series
Reconstruct from the components and compare with the original series
questions.explanation: The lecture recommends checking that the chosen component combination describes the observed series well.

questions.question: A pattern repeats every T seconds. How is its frequency f related to T?
choices: f = 1/T
f = T squared
f = T + 1
f is unrelated to T
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of repetitions per unit time, the inverse of period.

questions.question: A vibration repeats once every two seconds. What is its frequency?
choices: 2 Hz
0.5 Hz
4 Hz
questions.explanation: f = 1/T = 1/2 cycles per second = 0.5 Hz.

questions.question: What does a Fourier transform reveal about a time series?
choices: Only its minimum and maximum values
Only the number of missing timestamps
Its component frequencies and their relative amplitudes
The exact cause of every peak
questions.explanation: Fourier analysis represents a signal by oscillatory components at different frequencies and strengths.

questions.question: What is a frequency spectrum?
choices: A list of time-zone offsets
A table of class labels
A sequence of raw observations in date order
A view of how signal content is distributed across frequencies
questions.explanation: A spectrum displays the frequency components rather than only the original time-domain waveform.

questions.question: A power spectral density plot has a pronounced peak at one frequency. What is a reasonable interpretation?
choices: A relatively strong repeating component occurs at that frequency
The entire series must be constant
No other frequency can be present
The peak proves what physically caused the signal
questions.explanation: A strong spectral peak suggests substantial signal power at the corresponding repetition rate.

questions.question: Why can a spectrum reveal more than a single seasonal-period estimate?
choices: It removes every source of noise
It can reveal several frequency components in the same signal
It guarantees the signal is stationary
It identifies the cause of every component
questions.explanation: A signal can contain multiple repeated patterns; spectral analysis shows their frequencies together.

questions.question: What important detail may a power spectrum computed over an entire recording hide?
choices: Whether the data is numerical
The names of the sensors
When a frequency became stronger or weaker
The units of every raw observation
questions.explanation: A whole-recording spectrum summarises frequencies across the recording but does not localise their changes in time.

questions.question: What does the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) do?
choices: Shuffles the original time order
Replaces all measurements with their median
Computes one transform only for the full recording
Computes Fourier transforms over successive short time windows
questions.explanation: STFT divides the signal into windows and estimates the frequency content of each window.

questions.question: Which three quantities are displayed in a typical spectrogram?
choices: Time, frequency, and signal intensity
Mean, median, and mode
Latitude, longitude, and distance
Row count, class count, and p-value
questions.explanation: Time is commonly horizontal, frequency vertical, and intensity or power is shown by colour.

questions.question: What distinguishes a spectrogram from a whole-recording power spectrum?
choices: A spectrogram cannot show frequency
A spectrogram shows how frequency content changes over time
A spectrum must use category labels
A spectrogram proves the signal's physical cause
questions.explanation: The windowed spectra retain time information, making evolving frequencies visible.

questions.question: Why can short windows help analyse a signal that is not stationary over its full duration?
choices: They make every observation identical
They remove every trend without checking
The process may be approximately stable within each short window
They guarantee an exact global Fourier model
questions.explanation: A globally changing signal can be locally close enough to stationary for windowed frequency analysis.

questions.question: A wrist accelerometer records walking, then running. Which view is better for seeing when the movement frequency changed?
choices: One whole-recording spectrum only
A category-count pie chart
Only the mean acceleration
A spectrogram
questions.explanation: A spectrogram preserves time alongside frequency, revealing the transition from one cadence to another.

questions.question: If a spectrogram's legend assigns a time-frequency cell a high intensity, what does that mean?
choices: Greater strength of that frequency at that time
A later calendar date only
A different categorical label
A longer text description
questions.explanation: Colour encodes the strength or power at a time-frequency location; read the legend to confirm its scale.

questions.question: Which statement is FALSE about Fourier analysis of a changing time series?
choices: A transform can reveal repeating frequencies
One full-series spectrum tells you exactly when each frequency occurred
Windowed transforms can track changing frequency content
Frequency is the inverse of period
questions.explanation: A full-series spectrum lacks the timing of local frequency changes; a spectrogram adds that time dimension.

questions.question: Which information is geospatial?
choices: Only numerical model scores
Locations such as coordinates, addresses, or area boundaries
Only dates without locations
Only category names with no spatial reference
questions.explanation: Geospatial information is tied to places on Earth's surface, often with additional attributes.

questions.question: Which coordinate describes north-south position relative to the equator?
choices: Longitude
Altitude
Latitude
Time zone
questions.explanation: Latitude measures angular north-south position; the slide accidentally swaps the latitude and longitude direction labels.

questions.question: Which coordinate describes east-west position relative to the prime meridian?
choices: Longitude
Latitude
Elevation
Sampling frequency
questions.explanation: Longitude measures angular east-west position; the lecture's coordinate-format slide has these direction headings swapped.

questions.question: A location has latitude -26.2 degrees. Which hemisphere contains it?
choices: Northern
Eastern
Western
Southern
questions.explanation: Negative latitude indicates a location south of the equator.

questions.question: Why does a coordinate reference system or datum matter?
choices: It guarantees every map has the same colours
It defines how coordinates correspond to positions on Earth
It gives each building a sales price
It changes all vectors into raster images
questions.explanation: A datum and coordinate system establish the spatial reference used to interpret coordinate numbers.

questions.question: Which identifier refers to the widely used WGS84 geographic coordinate system?
choices: EPSG:3857 only
EPSG:4326
questions.explanation: WGS84 latitude/longitude coordinates are commonly identified by EPSG:4326.

questions.question: Two map layers represent the same city but plot in different positions. What should you check first?
choices: Whether their coordinate reference systems match or were transformed correctly
Whether both files have the same name
Whether both layers use the same colour
Whether the city has a seasonal trend
questions.explanation: Mismatched spatial references can make coordinates appear misaligned even when both layers describe the same place.

questions.question: Which set lists vector geometry types?
choices: Pixels, rows, and columns
Mean, median, and mode
Trend, seasonality, and noise
Points, lines, and polygons
questions.explanation: Vector spatial data represents features as discrete geometries such as points, lines, and polygons.

questions.question: What is raster spatial data?
choices: A list of only place names
A pixel or cell grid with values tied to locations
Only a road-network edge list
A shapefile geometry index
questions.explanation: Raster data is arranged in cells or pixels, as in satellite imagery or a measured spatial grid.

questions.question: A building polygon also records its use and construction year. What are those non-spatial details called?
choices: Attributes
A second coordinate system
Raster pixels
Autocorrelation lags
questions.explanation: Attributes describe a spatial feature beyond its geometry or location.

questions.question: In a shapefile dataset, what is stored in the .shp component?
choices: Only the colour legend
The index for geometry
Feature geometry
Only the timestamp format
questions.explanation: The .shp file stores the vector shapes themselves.

questions.question: What is the role of the .shx file alongside a shapefile's .shp file?
choices: It stores the main attribute table
It converts vector to raster
It defines the time zone
It indexes the feature geometries
questions.explanation: The .shx companion provides the geometry index.

questions.question: What information is stored in a shapefile's .dbf component?
choices: Only the polygon coordinates
The attributes associated with spatial features
The geographic prime meridian
A Fourier frequency spectrum
questions.explanation: The .dbf file stores the tabular non-spatial attributes for the shapes.

questions.question: For two locations a short distance apart, why can a flat-Earth distance approximation be reasonable?
choices: Earth's curvature has little effect over a small area
Latitude and longitude become metres
Both locations must share one latitude
The Earth stops rotating locally
questions.explanation: Over a small area, the curved surface is close enough to flat for an approximation, depending on the accuracy needed.

questions.question: You need the surface distance between two cities far apart on Earth. Which approach accounts for Earth's curvature?
choices: Subtract their longitude values and call the result kilometres
Count raster pixels without knowing their size
Use a great-circle calculation such as haversine
Treat the cities as adjacent cells
questions.explanation: Great-circle methods such as haversine account for the curved Earth; simple flat approximations become less suitable over larger distances.

questions.question: A difference of 1 in latitude or longitude is measured in what unit when using geographic coordinates?
choices: Kilometres
Degrees of angle
Raster cells
Seconds
questions.explanation: Geographic latitude and longitude are angles, not direct ground-distance units.

questions.question: Why does a 1-degree difference in longitude not always represent the same ground distance?
choices: Longitude is a time measure
Map colours change the distance
Height above sea level is its main cause
Meridians converge toward the poles, so distance varies with latitude
questions.explanation: Lines of longitude meet at the poles. Thus one degree of longitude spans less ground distance at higher latitudes.

questions.question: Which statement about computing distance directly from latitude/longitude degrees is most accurate?
choices: Subtracting coordinates always gives kilometres
Latitude and longitude have identical ground scales everywhere
Degree differences need an appropriate distance method or spatial conversion
Altitude alone converts degrees to metres
questions.explanation: Angular coordinates cannot simply be subtracted and interpreted as kilometres; choose a suitable geographic-distance method or projection.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of showing point data over a basemap with borders, roads, or imagery?
choices: It removes every missing value
It gives geographic context and helps reveal location errors
It guarantees a causal explanation
It changes all points into polygons
questions.explanation: A basemap shows where points fall relative to known places and can make implausible or misplaced points obvious.

questions.question: A set of South African locations appears north of the equator. Which coordinate issue should you investigate first?
choices: Too many shapefile attributes
Incorrect hemisphere or missing minus sign on latitude
A moving-average window that is too long
An overfitted random forest
questions.explanation: South Africa is in the Southern Hemisphere, so its latitude values should be negative.

questions.question: A location field defaults to (0, 0) when a real address cannot be mapped. How should a cluster at (0, 0) be interpreted?
choices: It proves many events occurred at the same real location
It proves the map projection is correct
It may be a missing or failed-geocoding placeholder that creates a false hotspot
It is the average of every valid coordinate
questions.explanation: A default coordinate can pile missing locations onto one map point and create a misleading concentration.

questions.question: A reporting system puts every unparsed address at its headquarters. What error can a point map show?
choices: An artificial hotspot at headquarters
A true increase in headquarters-area events
A guaranteed improvement in spatial precision
A change in Earth's curvature
questions.explanation: Defaulting failed addresses to one valid place falsely concentrates events there; the map can expose that artefact.

questions.question: GPS points are recorded in time order as a vehicle moves. Which plot best represents its trajectory?
choices: A pie chart of coordinate signs
An unordered histogram of latitudes
A map connecting the points in their recorded sequence
A single mean coordinate only
questions.explanation: A trajectory depends on the spatial points and their order, so connecting sequential points reveals the path.

questions.question: Why might connecting randomly scattered event locations in row order be misleading?
choices: Points cannot be shown on a map
The line would suggest a trajectory that the events do not represent
A basemap makes points invisible
Random locations have no coordinates
questions.explanation: Connecting points is meaningful when they form an ordered path, not merely because they occur as rows in a dataset.

questions.question: A map shades each South African province according to its total number of recorded accidents. What type of map is this?
choices: Trajectory map
Scatter plot
Choropleth map
Spectrogram
questions.explanation: A choropleth colours predefined geographic areas according to a statistic aggregated for each area.

questions.question: Which feature most clearly distinguishes a choropleth from a spatial heatmap?
choices: A choropleth shades defined areas; a heatmap shows spatial intensity beyond those fixed boundaries
Only a heatmap may use colours
A choropleth always shows individual GPS points
A heatmap must use province borders
questions.explanation: Choropleths summarise metrics inside chosen regions, while heatmaps convey intensity across space without requiring those region boundaries.

questions.question: Thousands of taxi pickup points overlap on a city map. Which display can show where pickups are most concentrated without drawing each point separately?
choices: A pie chart of coordinates
A boxplot of longitude only
An ADF test
A spatial intensity heatmap
questions.explanation: A heatmap aggregates the point pattern into a spatial intensity display.

questions.question: Province A has 100 accidents among 1 million people; Province B has 80 among 100,000 people. For comparing per-person accident risk, which value is more appropriate?
choices: Only the raw accident count
An accident rate adjusted for population
The province name in alphabetical order
The number of map pixels in each province
questions.explanation: Raw counts reflect how many events occurred, but rates account for the population at risk; B has fewer events yet a higher per-person rate.

questions.question: Two provinces have different population sizes. Why can a choropleth of raw case counts mislead a comparison of risk?
choices: Raw counts are always missing
Map shading changes the arithmetic
More people can produce more cases even when individual risk is lower
Choropleths cannot show numbers
questions.explanation: A larger population may have more total cases simply because more people are exposed; use a suitable rate when comparing risk.

questions.question: A province is shaded by its average income. What important detail can this area-level summary hide?
choices: Differences between neighbourhoods within the province
The province's existence
The units of latitude everywhere
Whether time has a past
questions.explanation: Aggregation gives one value for the whole area, which can mask substantial within-area variation.

questions.question: A map of taxi positions changes throughout the day. Which method helps reveal that change?
choices: Ignore every timestamp
Show only one map for all hours
Sort taxi names alphabetically
Make a map for each hour or animate the time periods
questions.explanation: Time slices or an animation preserve when points occurred instead of collapsing the whole day into one map.

questions.question: Morning and evening taxi hotspots differ. What might a single all-day heatmap conceal?
choices: That taxis have locations
When each hotspot was active
The map's north direction
Whether point data is vector data
questions.explanation: Combining all times can hide how the spatial pattern changes by hour; compare time slices to see when each hotspot forms.

questions.question: Can a map combine taxi point markers, a road network, and a separate summary of trip times?
choices: Yes, layers and linked summaries can provide complementary context
No, every map supports exactly one data type
Only if all taxis share one coordinate
Only after discarding timestamps
questions.explanation: Different spatial layers and time summaries can be combined to explain more than a single view.

questions.question: A road map colours segments by steepness rather than traffic density. What does this illustrate?
choices: Only event counts can be mapped
Colour must always encode latitude
Spatial displays can encode different numerical attributes
Steepness is necessarily a time series
questions.explanation: Map colour or intensity can represent numerical features such as road incline, not only point density or counts.

questions.question: A database stores street addresses but no coordinates. Which process can turn the addresses into points for a map?
choices: Differencing
Geocoding
Geofencing
Binning
questions.explanation: Geocoding converts a text address or place description into geographic coordinates.

questions.question: A GPS coordinate is available, but the analyst needs a nearby address or place name. What is this conversion called?
choices: Reverse geocoding
One-hot encoding
Great-circle routing
Standardisation
questions.explanation: Reverse geocoding starts with coordinates and seeks a human-readable address or place name.

questions.question: A street name occurs in two Johannesburg suburbs. Why should an automatically geocoded result be checked?
choices: All coordinates are measured in kilometres
A geocoder always returns (0, 0)
The same street name can lead to the wrong matching location
Geocoding can only process one-word addresses
questions.explanation: Ambiguous or incomplete addresses can match a real but incorrect place, so location plausibility matters.

questions.question: A vehicle alert is triggered when its GPS point enters a defined area. Which spatial idea is being used?
choices: Box-Cox transformation
Fourier decomposition
Mean imputation
Geofencing
questions.explanation: A geofence is a virtual boundary, and the system tests whether the GPS point lies inside it.

questions.question: To assign each clinic point to a municipality polygon, what spatial question must be answered?
choices: Which polygon contains each point?
Which clinic has the highest longitude?
Which points have identical timestamps?
What is the Fourier frequency of each point?
questions.explanation: Point-in-polygon testing identifies the boundary area containing each location.

questions.question: An activity app hides the start and end of a route within a short distance of the user's home. What is the purpose of this zone?
choices: To estimate the user's average speed
To protect a sensitive location with a spatial safety boundary
To convert all GPS points into street names
To calculate the shortest road route
questions.explanation: A safety zone suppresses points within a specified range of a private location, such as a home.

questions.question: In a road network, what do nodes and edges usually represent?
choices: Nodes are map colours; edges are time periods
Nodes are pixels; edges are rainfall values
Nodes are junctions or locations; edges are connecting road segments
Nodes are only countries; edges are only borders
questions.explanation: A network models connected places with nodes and the connections between them with edges.

questions.question: For a fastest-driving-route problem, what could a road edge's weight represent?
choices: The street name's number of letters
Travel time along that segment
The map background colour
The road's latitude sign
questions.explanation: Weighted edges can encode travel time; a shortest-distance task could instead use segment length.

questions.question: Why might a road-network edge need a direction?
choices: To make longitude positive
To produce a heatmap
To show a one-way street where travel is allowed in only one direction
To turn an address into coordinates
questions.explanation: Direction is needed when a connection can be traversed one way but not the reverse.

questions.question: Two addresses are close as the crow flies, but a river and one-way roads separate them. What should estimate their actual driving time?
choices: Only their straight-line distance
Only a latitude histogram
A road-network route using travel-time weights and directions
The area of the municipality polygon
questions.explanation: Driving time depends on connected roads, permitted direction, and road travel-time weights rather than straight-line distance alone.

questions.question: Neighbouring areas tend to have similarly high or similarly low house prices. What spatial pattern is this?
choices: Positive spatial autocorrelation
Negative spatial autocorrelation
No spatial information
A time-series unit root
questions.explanation: Positive spatial autocorrelation means nearby places tend to have similar attribute values.

questions.question: A map alternates high-value and low-value areas so neighbours tend to be unlike each other. Which description fits?
choices: Positive spatial autocorrelation
Negative spatial autocorrelation
A perfectly uniform attribute
A duplicate address
questions.explanation: Negative spatial autocorrelation means nearby areas tend to be dissimilar in the attribute being studied.

questions.question: What does a spatial-weights matrix specify?
choices: Which months belong to each season
Which attributes are categorical
Which locations count as neighbours and how strongly they are linked
Which point has the highest altitude only
questions.explanation: Spatial weights formalise neighbourhood relationships, for example using distance or shared boundaries.

questions.question: Two square areas touch only at one corner. Under which common contiguity rule are they neighbours?
choices: Rook only
Neither rook nor queen
Both rook and queen
Queen, but not rook
questions.explanation: Queen contiguity accepts a shared edge or corner; rook contiguity requires a shared edge.

questions.question: Under rook contiguity, when are two area polygons treated as neighbours?
choices: When they share an edge
Only when they share a corner
Whenever they have the same income
Whenever they share a map colour
questions.explanation: Rook contiguity uses shared edges, like a rook moving across adjacent squares on a chessboard.

questions.question: Instead of shared borders, an analyst gives nearby places larger weights than distant ones. Which spatial-weight approach is this?
choices: Time-window smoothing
Distance-based weighting
One-hot encoding
Rook-only contiguity
questions.explanation: Distance-based weights express spatial closeness by separation rather than a binary shared-border rule.

questions.question: A spatial lag of income is calculated for one neighbourhood. What does it summarise?
choices: The neighbourhood's income last year
Only its own income
The weighted income values of its neighbouring areas
The number of missing coordinates
questions.explanation: A spatial lag uses the spatial weights to summarise an attribute in surrounding locations.

questions.question: What question does global Moran's I address?
choices: Which exact street has the largest hotspot?
Whether the whole study area shows spatial association in an attribute
How to geocode a text address
Which road is shortest by driving time
questions.explanation: Global Moran's I summarises overall spatial autocorrelation, not the exact location of each hotspot.

questions.question: A statistically supported Moran's I is strongly positive. What does it suggest?
choices: Nearby areas tend to have similar values
Every area has the same value
Nearby areas tend to have opposite values
The map has no spatial coordinates
questions.explanation: A positive Moran's I indicates global clustering of similar values; significance helps distinguish that pattern from a random one.

questions.question: Moran's I is close to zero for a mapped attribute. What is the cautious interpretation?
choices: There must be one strong hotspot
All locations have equal values
There is little overall spatial autocorrelation under the chosen weights
The latitude and longitude were swapped
questions.explanation: Near zero indicates little global association for that weighting scheme; it does not rule out local patterns.

questions.question: A statistically supported Moran's I is negative. What does it suggest?
choices: Only that the data contain missing values
Neighbouring values tend to be dissimilar
A single all-area hotspot
A definite cause-and-effect relationship
questions.explanation: Negative global spatial autocorrelation means nearby attribute values tend to contrast.

questions.question: When testing whether observed spatial autocorrelation is unusual, what is the null hypothesis described in the lecture?
choices: Every value increases with time
Every pair of areas shares an edge
All points are at (0, 0)
Complete spatial randomness
questions.explanation: The lecture compares the observed pattern with a reference distribution under complete spatial randomness.

questions.question: Global Moran's I suggests overall clustering, but you need to identify where specific clusters are. What should you use?
choices: Only the global value again
LISA or another local spatial-association analysis
A non-spatial mean only
A time-series unit-root test
questions.explanation: Global Moran's I summarises the study area; local indicators such as LISA identify locations of local clusters and outliers.

questions.question: In a LISA classification, what does HH mean?
choices: A high-value area surrounded by high-value neighbours
A high-value area surrounded by low-value neighbours
A low-value area surrounded by low-value neighbours
An area with no neighbours
questions.explanation: High-high is a local cluster of high attribute values.

questions.question: In a LISA classification, what does LL indicate?
choices: A high area among low neighbours
A missing-coordinate placeholder
A low-value area with low-value neighbours
A low area among high neighbours
questions.explanation: Low-low identifies a cluster of low values, often called a coldspot for the measured attribute.

questions.question: An area has a high value but its surrounding areas have low values. Which LISA category fits?
choices: HH cluster
LL cluster
LH outlier
HL spatial outlier
questions.explanation: High-low (HL) is unlike its neighbours, so it is a local spatial outlier rather than a same-value cluster.

questions.question: A low-value area sits among high-value neighbours. How should it be classified by LISA?
choices: HH hotspot
LH spatial outlier
LL coldspot
No location can have this pattern
questions.explanation: Low-high (LH) contrasts with its high-value neighbours and is a spatial outlier.

questions.question: Which pair of LISA categories describes areas similar to their neighbours rather than local outliers?
choices: HL and LH
HH and HL
HH and LL
LH and LL
questions.explanation: HH and LL are like-neighbour clusters; HL and LH are unlike-neighbour outliers.

questions.question: Which clustering method usually requires choosing the number of groups k before fitting?
choices: K-means
HDBSCAN
Geocoding
Moran's I
questions.explanation: K-means partitions points into a chosen number k of clusters.

questions.question: A point dataset has irregularly shaped clusters and scattered noise. Which choice is especially suitable?
choices: K-means with a fixed k only
A choropleth without analysis
A global average coordinate
A density-based method such as HDBSCAN
questions.explanation: Density-based clustering can capture irregular shapes and treat scattered points as noise.

questions.question: What is one advantage of HDBSCAN over basic k-means for exploratory spatial clustering?
choices: It guarantees a fixed number of equal-sized circular groups
It can find varying-density clusters without preselecting k
It converts addresses into latitude and longitude
It calculates a province-wide Moran's I
questions.explanation: HDBSCAN uses density structure and does not require a chosen number of clusters in advance.

questions.question: Why might HDBSCAN label some points as noise rather than assign every point to a cluster?
choices: All points must be at (0, 0)
Only polygons can form clusters
Some points are not part of a sufficiently dense, stable region
Latitude is missing from every point
questions.explanation: Density-based methods can leave sparse or isolated points unclustered instead of forcing them into a group.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of dimensionality reduction?
choices: To retain useful information while representing the data with fewer dimensions
To duplicate every original feature in a new coordinate system
To guarantee that every machine-learning model is perfectly accurate
To remove all variation from the data
questions.explanation: Dimensionality reduction seeks a smaller representation that preserves as much useful information as possible while discarding less useful structure.

questions.question: Why is high-dimensional data difficult for people to interpret directly?
choices: People can only calculate covariance for one variable
People can readily visualise two or three dimensions, but not many dimensions
High-dimensional data never contains patterns
Every high-dimensional dataset is categorical
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts the ease of visualising two or three dimensions with the difficulty of interpreting many dimensions directly.

questions.question: Which of the following is a computational reason to reduce dimensionality?
choices: More features always require less memory and less processing
Computations can become expensive when a dataset has many features
Dimensionality reduction converts every algorithm into a linear one
Fewer features guarantee that no data cleaning is needed
questions.explanation: Working with many features can increase computational cost, so a smaller representation can make later processing more efficient.

questions.question: Which modelling problem becomes easier to encounter as the number of features grows?
choices: Underflow in every covariance calculation
Overfitting
Perfect linear separability
Guaranteed independence between variables
questions.explanation: The lecture lists overfitting as one of the risks associated with high-dimensional data.

questions.question: Why is randomly dropping variables a poor dimensionality-reduction strategy?
choices: It may discard variables containing important information
It always increases the number of dimensions
It forces the covariance matrix to become rectangular
It makes every remaining feature categorical
questions.explanation: Random removal provides no protection against losing important information carried by the discarded variables.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes feature elimination?
choices: Removing explicit features from the dataset
Replacing every feature with a class label
Creating only nonlinear latent variables
Sorting observations by their target value
questions.explanation: Feature elimination removes original features directly, which can also remove the information those features contributed.

questions.question: What is a central difference between feature elimination and dimensionality reduction by feature extraction?
choices: Feature elimination removes original variables, while extraction forms new variables from combinations of them
Feature elimination is supervised, while extraction is always unsupervised
Feature elimination adds dimensions, while extraction preserves the exact original dimensions
Feature elimination uses covariance, while extraction cannot use covariance
questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes dropping explicit variables from forming new extracted variables that combine information from the originals.

questions.question: In the lecture's description of dimensionality reduction, how are extracted features selected?
choices: A subset is retained after ranking the new features by predictive power
Every extracted feature is retained regardless of usefulness
The features are selected alphabetically
Only the original feature with the largest name is retained
questions.explanation: The lecture describes keeping a subset of newly engineered or extracted features ranked by their predictive power.

questions.question: Why can an extracted feature preserve useful parts of several original variables?
choices: It can be a combination of multiple original variables
It must be identical to one original variable
It removes all covariance before it is calculated
It assigns the same value to every observation
questions.explanation: An extracted feature can combine contributions from multiple original variables instead of retaining or dropping each one as a whole.

questions.question: What does a larger variance indicate about a variable?
choices: Its observations are more spread out
Its observations are all identical
It is necessarily independent of every other variable
It has a negative correlation with the target
questions.explanation: Variance measures spread; larger variance indicates that the observations are more dispersed.

questions.question: What does a positive covariance between two variables suggest?
choices: They tend to change in similar directions
They must have identical means
One is categorical and the other is continuous
They are guaranteed to have a causal relationship
