questions.explanation: Positive covariance indicates similar directional behaviour: as one variable changes, the other tends to change in the same direction.

questions.question: Why is the magnitude of covariance difficult to interpret by itself?
choices: Covariance is not normalised and depends on the scales of the variables
Covariance can only equal zero or one
Covariance is defined only for class labels
Covariance always has the same units as correlation
questions.explanation: Because covariance is not normalised, its magnitude is scale-dependent; correlation is easier to interpret as a standardised measure.

questions.question: What does an entry in a covariance matrix represent?
choices: The covariance between the variables named by its row and column
The number of missing values in one observation
The predicted class of a single observation
The rank of an eigenvalue after sorting
questions.explanation: Rows and columns correspond to features, and each entry gives the covariance of the associated pair.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about independence and correlation is TRUE?
choices: Independence implies no correlation, but no correlation does not necessarily imply independence
No correlation always proves that two variables are independent
Correlation proves that one variable causes the other
Independent variables must have identical distributions
questions.explanation: The lecture stresses the one-way implication: independence implies no correlation, but uncorrelated variables need not be independent.

questions.question: Which equation defines an eigenvector $v$ of a matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$?
choices: $Av = \lambda v$
$A + v = \lambda$
$A = v + \lambda$
$vA = v - \lambda$
questions.explanation: An eigenvector keeps its direction under the matrix transformation, with the eigenvalue giving its scale factor.

questions.question: What does linear separability mean for a two-class, two-dimensional dataset?
choices: A straight line can completely separate the two classes
Every variable has zero variance
The classes have identical centroids
A curved boundary is required to separate the classes
questions.explanation: In two dimensions, linear separability means a straight line can separate the classes; in higher dimensions the boundary is a hyperplane.

questions.question: What is the higher-dimensional equivalent of a separating line?
choices: A hyperplane
A histogram
A covariance scalar
A scree point
questions.explanation: A hyperplane generalises a separating line to higher-dimensional spaces.

questions.question: Which approach is most direct for checking linear separation when there are only two features?
choices: Plot the data and inspect whether a line separates the classes
Apply blind source separation without looking at labels
Increase the data to ten dimensions
Assume the data is linear without checking
questions.explanation: With very few dimensions, a plot can make linear separation directly visible.

questions.question: For labelled classification data, why can a support vector machine be useful as a linearity check?
choices: It attempts to separate classes using a hyperplane
It guarantees that all features are independent
It computes only the mean of each feature
It converts nonlinear data into survey factors
questions.explanation: A linear support vector machine looks for a separating hyperplane, which directly relates to linear separability.

questions.question: How can a simple classifier act as a sanity check before applying linear dimensionality reduction?
choices: Good performance can indicate that useful linear structure is present
Poor performance proves that no pattern of any kind exists
It makes standardisation unnecessary
It calculates the latent survey factors directly
questions.explanation: The lecture suggests that a basic linear model can reveal whether it can exploit linear structure, while noting that one can also apply PCA and inspect the result.

questions.question: Which correlation measure is associated with linear correlation in the lecture?
choices: Pearson correlation
Spearman correlation
Moran's I
Factor loading
questions.explanation: The lecture associates Pearson correlation with linear correlation and Spearman correlation with non-linear or rank-based association.

questions.question: Which correlation measure is suggested for a non-linear monotonic relationship?
choices: Spearman correlation
Pearson correlation only
An eigenvalue
A scree plot
questions.explanation: The lecture lists Spearman's measure for non-linear relationships.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about correlation is TRUE?
choices: Correlation does not by itself imply causation
A strong correlation always identifies the causal direction
Only negatively correlated variables can be independent
Correlation and covariance are identical without any scaling difference
questions.explanation: A relationship between variables does not establish that one causes the other.

questions.question: What is the purpose of eigendecomposition in the lecture's description?
choices: To factor a matrix into eigenvalues and eigenvectors
To sort observations by their class label
To replace all features with their means
To turn a rectangular matrix into a text label
questions.explanation: Eigendecomposition represents a matrix through its eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

questions.question: What does the magnitude of an eigenvalue indicate about its eigenvector component?
choices: How strongly the matrix stretches or shrinks that direction
The number of class labels in the dataset
The feature's original measurement unit only
Whether the variable is categorical
questions.explanation: The eigenvalue is the scale factor applied to its eigenvector direction; a larger value generally indicates a larger contribution.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes singular value decomposition from eigendecomposition?
choices: SVD does not require the matrix to be diagonalizable
SVD can only be used on one-dimensional data
Eigendecomposition works only with class labels
SVD produces no matrix factors
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that SVD provides a decomposition without requiring diagonalizability in the way eigendecomposition does.

questions.question: Which expression represents the singular value decomposition shown in the lecture?
choices: $A = U\Sigma V^T$
$A = X + Y$
$A = \lambda + v$
$A = F/A$
questions.explanation: SVD factors a matrix into left singular vectors, a diagonal singular-value matrix, and transposed right singular vectors.

questions.question: What does Principal Component Analysis primarily seek?
choices: Linear combinations of variables that explain as much variance as possible
Class labels that have identical covariance matrices
A nonlinear boundary that perfectly classifies every observation
A random subset of unchanged original features
questions.explanation: PCA projects the data onto linear combinations chosen to capture maximum variance.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes PCA?
choices: A projection-based method that transforms data into a lower-dimensional space
A method that deletes observations with small target values
A supervised classifier designed only for binary labels
A method that preserves every original feature unchanged
questions.explanation: PCA is a projection method: it changes the coordinate system and can retain a lower-dimensional subset of the resulting components.

questions.question: How are the first and second principal components related?
choices: The first captures maximum variance, and the second captures remaining variance while being uncorrelated with the first
The second always captures more variance than the first
They are required to be identical
Both are chosen using class labels
questions.explanation: Principal components are ordered by captured variance, and later components are uncorrelated with earlier ones.

questions.question: What do the direction and magnitude of a principal component represent?
choices: Direction gives the principal axis, while magnitude reflects the variance captured along it
Direction gives the class label, while magnitude gives the number of observations
Direction gives the feature name, while magnitude gives its measurement unit
Direction gives the survey question, while magnitude gives the response text
questions.explanation: A principal component defines a direction in feature space and an amount of variance captured when the data is projected onto it.

questions.question: Why is PCA considered an unsupervised method?
choices: It finds variance directions without using class labels
It requires a labelled target for every observation
It maximises separation between known classes
It can only run after fitting a classifier
questions.explanation: PCA uses the structure of the feature data and does not use class membership when choosing components.

questions.question: If the main goal is to visualise a high-dimensional dataset, how many principal components are usually retained?
choices: Two or three
Exactly one hundred
All components without exception
Zero components
questions.explanation: Two or three components are practical for visualisation because people can directly view two- or three-dimensional plots.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a scree plot in PCA?
choices: To compare the variance explained by successive components
To display the original class labels in alphabetical order
To prove that every feature is independent
To detect missing values in each observation
questions.explanation: A scree plot shows how much variance is associated with each component and helps choose how many to retain.

questions.question: What assumption motivates PCA's focus on high-variance directions?
choices: High variability often represents signal, while low variability often represents noise
Low variability always identifies the target class perfectly
Every high-variance feature is causal
Variance is unrelated to information
questions.explanation: PCA treats directions with more variability as more likely to contain important signal, while recognising this is an assumption.

questions.question: Why should features be standardised before PCA?
choices: Features measured on larger numerical scales could otherwise dominate the variance
PCA can only accept values between zero and one
Standardisation supplies the missing class labels
Standardisation guarantees that the data is nonlinear
questions.explanation: Because PCA maximises variance, scale differences can make a feature appear important simply because of its units.

questions.question: How does the fitting criterion illustrated for PCA differ from ordinary regression?
choices: PCA considers orthogonal distances to the fitted direction
PCA minimises only vertical prediction errors for a chosen dependent variable
PCA requires the response variable to be categorical
PCA fits no direction through the data
questions.explanation: The slide contrasts regressing one variable on another with PCA's orthogonal projection relative to the principal direction.

questions.question: In the PCA procedure, what should be done to the columns of the original matrix $X$ first?
choices: Centre them to mean zero and, for full standardisation, scale them to variance one
Sort them alphabetically by feature name
Replace them with class labels
Delete every column with non-zero variance
questions.explanation: The first stated step is to standardise the feature columns so that scale does not distort the variance comparison.

questions.question: For centred data with observations in rows and variables in columns, what does $X^T X$ represent up to the factor $1/(n-1)$?
choices: The covariance matrix
The class-confusion matrix
The vector of target labels
The matrix of survey text responses
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies $X^T X/(n-1)$ as the covariance matrix for centred data.

questions.question: After decomposing the covariance matrix, how are its eigenvalues used in PCA?
choices: They are sorted in descending order together with their corresponding eigenvectors
They are discarded before the components are calculated
They are sorted by the names of the original variables
They are converted into class labels
questions.explanation: Sorting eigenvalues from largest to smallest orders the directions by the variance they capture, while the eigenvectors must remain aligned with them.

questions.question: If $P^*$ is the matrix of sorted eigenvectors, how are the principal-component scores calculated?
choices: $X^* = X - \lambda$
questions.explanation: Multiplying the standardised data by the sorted eigenvector matrix projects each observation into principal-component coordinates.

questions.question: Which property of PCA output makes it useful for decorrelation or whitening?
choices: The principal components are uncorrelated
The original features remain duplicated
Every component has the same eigenvalue
The class labels are evenly balanced
questions.explanation: PCA produces orthogonal, uncorrelated component directions, which can be used as a decorrelated representation.

questions.question: Which data problem can strongly distort PCA?
choices: Outliers
Balanced class labels
A descriptive feature name
A fixed random seed
questions.explanation: PCA is highly susceptible to outliers because extreme observations can dominate variance and therefore the selected directions.

questions.question: Why can ordinary PCA be difficult to apply to a massive dataset?
choices: It reads all of the data into memory at once
It requires every feature to be text
It cannot calculate more than two components
It must use a labelled target
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies the need to load the full data as a limitation for very large datasets.

questions.question: What is the role of Randomised SVD in the lecture?
choices: It provides an approximate, iterative decomposition for large data
It guarantees an exact nonlinear separation
It replaces standardisation with class labels
It converts PCA into Factor Analysis
questions.explanation: Randomised SVD is presented as an approximate iterative alternative whose principal components are updated during iterations.

questions.question: What happens if ordinary linear PCA is applied to data whose important separation is nonlinear?
choices: It may fail to find the separation
It always converts the data into perfectly separated classes
It automatically becomes a nonlinear classifier
It guarantees a higher target accuracy
questions.explanation: PCA is a linear transformation, so nonlinear structure may not be captured by its component directions.

questions.question: Why was PCA useful for visualising the Iris dataset in the lecture?
choices: It reduced four measured dimensions to a small number of components that could be plotted
It added four new class labels to every flower
It removed all variation between flower species
It changed every measurement into a survey response
questions.explanation: The Iris data has four measurement features, which are hard to picture directly; PCA provides a two-dimensional projection.

questions.question: Approximately how much variance did two principal components capture in the lecture's Iris example?
questions.explanation: The slide reports that two principal components captured about 95% of the variance in the Iris dataset.

questions.question: Which Iris measurement mainly influenced the second principal component in the lecture example?
choices: Sepal width
Petal width only
The flower class label
The observation number
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that the first component was influenced by sepal length and petal measurements, while the second was mostly influenced by sepal width.

questions.question: In the Boston housing example, what happened to cumulative explained variance as more components were added?
choices: It increased
It immediately became zero
It became a class label
It decreased below the variance of the first component
questions.explanation: Adding components retains additional variance, so cumulative explained variance increases.

questions.question: Which set of explained-variance values matches the Boston housing example?
choices: One component: 45%; two components: 58%; five components: 80%
One component: 80%; two components: 58%; five components: 45%
One component: 10%; two components: 20%; five components: 30%
One component: 100%; two components: 100%; five components: 100%
questions.explanation: The slide reports 45% for the first component, 58% cumulatively for two, and 80% cumulatively for five.

questions.question: What did the colours represent in the Boston housing principal-component plot?
choices: A sliding scale of median house prices
Three known flower classes
The order in which rows were loaded
The number of missing values in each feature
questions.explanation: Because the target was continuous rather than categorical, colour represented median house price on a continuous scale.

questions.question: What did the lecture suggest doing to make the Boston PCA plot easier to interpret by target group?
choices: Bin the continuous house prices to create target categories
Remove the target variable permanently
Duplicate every observation
Replace the principal components with random values
questions.explanation: Binning the continuous target into categories was suggested as a way to make group patterns clearer.

questions.question: How can PCA reduce the training cost of a machine-learning model?
choices: Use a smaller set of principal components as the model inputs
Increase the number of original pixels used by the model
Train a separate model for every original feature
Replace the training data with class names only
questions.explanation: A model can train on fewer component features than the original high-dimensional representation.

questions.question: In the MNIST example, what original dimensionality was reduced by PCA?
choices: 784 pixel features
Four flower measurements
Three survey factors
Two audio sources
questions.explanation: The handwritten-image representation used 784 pixels, which PCA compressed into fewer component inputs.

questions.question: Why could classification accuracy decrease when all variance was retained instead of retaining 80% in the MNIST example?
choices: Additional components could reintroduce noise or spurious correlations
PCA cannot produce more than one component
The class labels were removed from the test set
Standardisation makes accuracy decrease by definition
questions.explanation: The lecture uses this result to show that discarded low-value directions may contain noise or spurious signal rather than useful predictive information.

questions.question: What is the fundamental aim of Factor Analysis?
choices: To identify latent variables that help explain observed variables
To maximise class separation using labelled data
To select the observations with the largest targets
To retain only the original variable with the highest variance
questions.explanation: Factor Analysis models observed measurements as arising from one or more unobserved latent factors.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares PCA and Factor Analysis?
choices: PCA forms components from observed variables, while Factor Analysis explains observed variables using latent factors
PCA and Factor Analysis use class labels in exactly the same way
Factor Analysis can only be applied to image pixels
PCA assumes every observed variable is a survey response
questions.explanation: PCA expresses components as weighted combinations of observations' features; Factor Analysis models observed features as effects of latent factors.

questions.question: In the Factor Analysis expression $X = AF$, what does $A$ represent?
choices: A mixing matrix describing the relationship between variables and factors
The vector of class labels
The sorted list of observation names
The covariance error for one feature only
questions.explanation: The mixing matrix contains the weights or loadings connecting the latent factors to the observed variables.

questions.question: Which property does the lecture assign to the factors in Factor Analysis?
choices: They are uncorrelated
They must be class labels
They must equal the original features
They must be ordered by observation time
questions.explanation: The lecture describes the latent factors in the Factor Analysis model as uncorrelated.

questions.question: What does Factor Analysis explain, in contrast with PCA's focus on maximum variance?
choices: Covariance shared among observed variables
The exact target value for every observation
Only the largest original feature
The nonlinear decision boundary of a classifier
questions.explanation: Factor Analysis looks for latent structure that accounts for covariance among observed variables, whereas PCA focuses on total variance.

questions.question: Which statement about orthogonality is TRUE according to the lecture?
choices: Factor Analysis does not require the same orthogonality condition as PCA
Factor Analysis requires every observed variable to be perpendicular to its factor
PCA allows all components to be correlated
Neither method uses linear combinations
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies the lack of a required orthogonality constraint as a mathematical distinction for Factor Analysis.

questions.question: What is a major practical benefit of Factor Analysis over PCA?
choices: Its factors can be interpretable as underlying constructs
It guarantees perfect classification accuracy
It never requires any assumptions
It always retains every original variable
questions.explanation: Latent factors can correspond to interpretable constructs, which is why Factor Analysis is widely used with survey data.

questions.question: When is Factor Analysis more appropriate than PCA?
choices: When testing whether latent factors may be causing patterns in observed variables
When the only goal is to rank class labels alphabetically
When every observed variable must remain unchanged
When there are no correlations among any variables
questions.explanation: Factor Analysis is suited to hypotheses about unobserved constructs that produce correlations among measured variables.

questions.question: If the goal is simply to reduce dimensionality into uncorrelated component variables, which method does the lecture recommend?
choices: PCA
Factor Analysis only
Linear Discriminant Analysis using no labels
A random feature deletion
questions.explanation: The lecture recommends PCA when the goal is straightforward dimensionality reduction into uncorrelated components rather than identifying latent constructs.

questions.question: What was the purpose of applying Factor Analysis to the airline survey responses?
choices: To find common latent themes across ratings of different service aspects
To predict the flight number from passenger names
To replace every rating with the overall mean
To create a nonlinear image classifier
questions.explanation: The survey example searches for common underlying constructs that explain groups of correlated service ratings.

questions.question: Based on the steep drop in eigenvalues in the survey example, how many factors were considered reasonable?
choices: Three or four
Exactly fourteen
Zero
At least one hundred
questions.explanation: The slide suggests three or four factors because the eigenvalue curve drops steeply through that region.

questions.question: In the survey loading matrix, what do the rows and columns represent?
choices: Rows are survey variables and columns are latent factors
Rows are class labels and columns are observations
Rows are eigenvalues and columns are file names
Rows are principal components and columns are target bins
questions.explanation: Each row corresponds to an observed survey question, and each column gives the loadings for one factor.

questions.question: Which ratings loaded strongly together on the first survey factor?
choices: Food and drink, seat comfort, inflight entertainment and cleanliness
Flight number, passenger surname, ticket barcode and gate code
Only departure time and arrival time
Only baggage weight and aircraft speed
questions.explanation: Those four service ratings had large loadings on the first factor and were interpreted as a possible hospitality or comfort construct.

questions.question: Why was a label such as “hospitality” or “comfort” proposed for the first survey factor?
choices: Several strongly loaded service ratings shared that underlying theme
The factor was explicitly asked as one survey question
The factor had the smallest possible eigenvalue
The factor was the passenger's class label
questions.explanation: The latent construct was inferred from the common meaning of the observed variables with large loadings, not measured directly.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)?
choices: A supervised linear method that can be used for classification and dimensionality reduction
An unsupervised method that ignores all class labels
A nonlinear clustering method for arbitrary shapes
A method used only to standardise feature scales
questions.explanation: LDA was developed as a classifier and is also used as a supervised linear transformation for dimensionality reduction.

questions.question: What is the key objective difference between LDA and PCA?
choices: LDA maximises separation between classes, while PCA maximises variance without using class labels
LDA maximises total variance, while PCA maximises class separation
Both methods ignore class labels and optimise the same objective
PCA is a classifier, while LDA cannot classify
questions.explanation: LDA uses labels to find discriminant directions that separate classes; PCA finds high-variance directions regardless of labels.

questions.question: What form do LDA's reduced features take?
choices: Linear combinations of the input features
Copies of the target labels only
Randomly selected unchanged observations
Nonlinear clusters with no class information
questions.explanation: Like PCA, LDA outputs linear combinations of input features, but it chooses them using a class-separation objective.

questions.question: According to the lecture, why should LDA not be used as an input transformation for a later regression problem?
choices: LDA is itself a classification technique built around class separation
LDA produces only missing values
LDA cannot form linear combinations
LDA always increases dimensionality
questions.explanation: The lecture cautions that LDA's discriminants are tied to classification rather than a continuous regression objective.

questions.question: Which statement about standardisation before LDA is TRUE?
choices: It is not strictly required, but it is generally a good idea
It is forbidden because LDA requires raw units
It replaces the need for class labels
It guarantees identical class covariance matrices
questions.explanation: The lecture says standardisation is not mandatory for LDA, although applying it is generally advisable.

questions.question: Which collection lists the assumptions stated for LDA classification?
choices: Normally distributed data, statistically independent features and identical covariance matrices across classes
Non-Gaussian sources, nonlinear mixing and dependent components
No labels, arbitrary cluster shapes and unequal feature lengths
Only binary features, zero variance and no covariance
questions.explanation: Those are the three assumptions listed for LDA when used as a classifier.

questions.question: When might PCA outperform LDA on a multiclass problem according to the lecture?
choices: When there are few samples per class
When every class has infinitely many samples
When the data contains no measured features
When the only goal is blind source separation
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that PCA can outperform LDA when the number of samples available for each class is small.

questions.question: How are PCA and LDA often combined?
choices: PCA first reduces dimensionality, and its outputs are then fed into LDA
LDA first removes all labels, and PCA recreates them
Both are run only to increase the number of features
PCA replaces every LDA discriminant with a random value
questions.explanation: PCA can first compress the feature space before LDA finds class-separating directions.

questions.question: Which limitation does LDA share with PCA according to the lecture?
choices: It relies on linear structure and may struggle to converge on very large data
It can only process survey responses
It cannot produce any reduced features
It requires every variable to be categorical
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights linearity and convergence on very large datasets as limitations, with regularised variants as possible alternatives.

questions.question: Which measures can be used to inspect an LDA dimensionality-reduction result?
choices: Scree plots, eigenvalues, eigenvectors and explained variance
Only file size and row order
Only the names of the class labels
Only the number of missing strings
questions.explanation: The lecture says the same kinds of component diagnostics used with PCA can also help assess LDA.

questions.question: Why can PCA fail to separate classes even when it captures directions of high variance?
choices: The largest variance may occur within every class in a similar way and therefore be useless for class separation
PCA always uses class labels incorrectly
PCA removes every high-variance direction
Class separation is identical to total variance by definition
questions.explanation: A feature can vary greatly overall yet have similar variation in every class, so it contributes little to distinguishing those classes.

questions.question: What did the Iris and wine examples illustrate about LDA?
choices: Its leading discriminant can find an axis that separates labelled classes
It always finds the same axes as PCA
It ignores all class information
It is designed to maximise variance within each class only
questions.explanation: The examples show LDA choosing directions for class separation, which can differ sharply from PCA's high-variance directions.

questions.question: What does Independent Component Analysis (ICA) do to a multivariate signal?
choices: Decomposes it into additive components while maximising their independence
Assigns every observation to a known class
Keeps only the variable with the largest variance
Sorts the samples by time without transforming them
questions.explanation: ICA seeks additive source components that are as statistically independent as possible.

questions.question: Which task is most strongly associated with ICA?
choices: Blind source separation of superimposed signals
Choosing the number of clusters for k-means
Calculating a class-confusion matrix
Binning a continuous house-price target
questions.explanation: ICA is commonly used to recover underlying sources from observed mixtures, as in the cocktail-party example.

questions.question: Which of the following could be a source signal in an ICA problem?
choices: An image, an audio signal or an EEG time series
Only a categorical class name
Only a covariance scalar
Only the row count of a dataset
questions.explanation: The lecture lists images, audio and time-series signals such as EEG as possible sources for ICA.

questions.question: How does ICA's latent-factor criterion differ from the Factor Analysis criterion described in the lecture?
choices: ICA seeks statistically independent factors rather than merely uncorrelated factors
ICA requires every factor to be a class label
ICA permits only one observed variable
ICA maximises total variance without considering independence
questions.explanation: ICA strengthens the requirement from lack of correlation to statistical independence between recovered sources.

questions.question: Why is whitening applied before ICA?
choices: To remove correlations as a necessary step toward statistical independence
To create class labels from continuous targets
To make all source signals Gaussian
To increase the number of observed mixtures
questions.explanation: Whitening removes correlations, which is necessary but not sufficient for the stronger goal of independence.

questions.question: Which set lists the three main ICA assumptions from the lecture?
choices: Linear mixing, mutually independent sources and non-Gaussian sources
Nonlinear mixing, identical sources and Gaussian sources
Labelled classes, equal covariance matrices and zero variance
Random feature removal, categorical inputs and fixed cluster count
questions.explanation: ICA assumes a linear mixture of independent, non-Gaussian source signals.

questions.question: Why would ICA be ineffective if the latent source factors were normally distributed?
choices: ICA relies on the sources being non-Gaussian to identify independent components
Gaussian sources always have class labels
Normal distributions make matrix multiplication impossible
ICA requires every source to have zero observations
questions.explanation: Non-Gaussianity is a core identifiability assumption for ICA; the lecture contrasts long-tailed ICA components with more Gaussian PCA components.

questions.question: What does the cocktail-party example demonstrate about ICA?
choices: It can recover separate source signals from observed mixtures
It can maximise class separation without any signals
It always produces the same components as PCA
It can only reduce survey data to one factor
questions.explanation: The example illustrates blind source separation: ICA attempts to recover the individual conversations or signals that were mixed together.

questions.question: When does the lecture suggest logistic regression as a possible linearity check?
choices: When the data has relatively low dimensionality and model accuracy can be inspected
When the data contains no target labels
Only after ICA has recovered non-Gaussian sources
Only when every feature has zero variance
questions.explanation: For lower-dimensional labelled data, the performance of a simple logistic regression model can provide evidence of useful linear structure.

questions.question: What property makes a simple perceptron relevant to checking linearity?
choices: It converges when the training data is linearly separable
It always discovers latent survey factors
It measures only nonlinear rank correlation
It guarantees convergence for every non-linear dataset
questions.explanation: The perceptron convergence property links successful convergence to linear separability, although the lecture cautions about using this idea in high dimensions.

questions.question: Under what condition does the lecture suggest clustering might help inspect structure before linear reduction?
choices: When there are relatively few features, such as fewer than ten
Only when there are millions of features
Only when every observation has the same value
When the number of classes is unknown but every feature is text
questions.explanation: The lecture lists clustering as a possible exploratory check when the feature count is relatively small.

questions.question: Which expression for the covariance of a random vector $X$ appears in the lecture?
choices: $E[XX^T] - E[X]E[X^T]$
$X^T/X$
$E[X]E[X^T] - E[XX^T]^2$
questions.explanation: The covariance matrix is expressed as $E[XX^T] - E[X]E[X^T]$, with the centred-data calculation often abbreviated using $XX^T$.

questions.question: What does the diagonal matrix $\Sigma$ contain in the SVD description from the lecture?
choices: Singular values related to square roots of eigenvalues
The original class labels
Only the means of the input columns
The names of the latent factors
questions.explanation: The lecture describes $\Sigma$ as a diagonal matrix of singular values related to square roots of eigenvalues.

questions.question: What distributional assumption does the lecture associate with the latent variable in Factor Analysis?
choices: A Gaussian distribution
A distribution that must have no variance
A categorical distribution with exactly two labels
A distribution that must match every observed feature exactly
questions.explanation: The lecture presents the unobserved factor as an underlying Gaussian variable influencing the observed measurements.

questions.question: From the mathematical perspective stated in the lecture, how can PCA be classified relative to Factor Analysis?
choices: PCA can be viewed as a specific type of factor analysis
PCA and Factor Analysis have no mathematical relationship
Factor Analysis is a supervised form of LDA
PCA is a nonlinear form of ICA
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that, despite their conceptual differences, PCA can technically be viewed as a specific type of factor analysis.

questions.question: When are LDA's classification assumptions described as less critical in the lecture?
choices: When LDA is being used for dimensionality reduction rather than classification
When LDA is being used with no measured features
When every class label is deleted
When LDA is replaced by a random projection
questions.explanation: The lecture says the assumptions, particularly feature independence, are less of an issue when LDA is used as a dimensionality-reduction technique.

questions.question: In the sports-team analogy, why could player height be emphasised by PCA but be useless for separating teams?
choices: Height could vary greatly overall while having the same range within every team
PCA can only process team names
Height would necessarily have zero variance
LDA and PCA always select identical directions
questions.explanation: High total variance does not guarantee between-class differences; the same height variation in every team would provide little discriminatory information.

questions.question: Which visual contrast between PCA and ICA components is highlighted in the handwritten-digit example?
choices: PCA components appear more multivariate normal, while ICA components have longer tails
PCA components are always categorical, while ICA components are always binary
PCA components have no variance, while ICA components are identical
PCA and ICA components have exactly the same distributions
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts the more Gaussian appearance of PCA components with the long-tailed, non-Gaussian character sought by ICA.

questions.question: What implicit assumption allows a linear method such as PCA to give a useful low-dimensional representation?
choices: Every feature is categorical
All observations have identical values
The class labels form a nonlinear boundary
The data can be represented well in a lower-dimensional linear subspace
questions.explanation: PCA searches for a flat linear projection, so it works best when the important structure can be represented by a lower-dimensional linear subspace.

questions.question: Why can PCA give a poor approximation of nonlinear data?
choices: PCA always deletes the largest eigenvalue
PCA requires every point to be an outlier
No line or plane may represent the curved structure well
PCA can only process text features
questions.explanation: PCA produces a linear approximation; a curved structure may not be captured by any flat line or plane.

questions.question: How does the manifold hypothesis generalise the assumption used by linear dimensionality reduction?
choices: It requires the lower-dimensional space to contain more dimensions than the input
It allows the lower-dimensional space to be curved and embedded in the higher-dimensional feature space
It assumes all pairwise distances are zero
It removes the need for any relationship between nearby points
questions.explanation: The manifold hypothesis assumes that high-dimensional observations lie on or near a lower-dimensional curved space embedded in the original feature space.

questions.question: Which method illustrates making a linear dimensionality-reduction method nonlinear?
choices: Kernel PCA
Ordinary least-squares regression
K-means with no features
A covariance table
questions.explanation: The lecture names Kernel PCA as an example of taking a linear method and nonlinearising it.

questions.question: What is the second broad non-parametric approach to nonlinear dimensionality reduction described in the lecture?
choices: Randomly remove original variables
Force the manifold to be globally flat
Replace all observations with their mean
Estimate the manifold and use properties measured along it
questions.explanation: Instead of modifying a linear method, one can estimate the underlying manifold and work with its geometry.

questions.question: Which distinction is made between nonlinear dimensionality-reduction methods?
choices: Some require data and others require no input
Some calculate variance and others cannot use numbers
Some provide a reusable mapping to an embedding, while others mainly provide a visualisation
Some preserve all dimensions and others add class labels
questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes methods that map new high-dimensional points into an embedding from methods used mainly for visualisation.

questions.question: Which method is mentioned as an example that may provide a visualisation rather than a general mapping?
choices: Kernel PCA
t-SNE
Ordinary PCA
Linear regression
questions.explanation: The lecture uses t-SNE as the example of a method that is primarily able to provide a visualisation.

questions.question: What does the Swiss roll example demonstrate about PCA?
choices: A flat PCA projection can fail to separate data that lies on a curved manifold
PCA always preserves curved geodesic distances
PCA turns every manifold into a similarity graph
PCA requires a hexagonal output grid
questions.explanation: The rolled surface is nonlinear, so flattening it with a linear projection does not preserve its structure well.

questions.question: What is the intended advantage of a manifold method on the Swiss roll?
choices: It assigns random class labels to the points
It maximises only the largest original coordinate
It makes all high-dimensional distances equal
It can unfold the curved surface while preserving meaningful distances along it
questions.explanation: A manifold method seeks an embedding that respects the geometry of the curved surface.

questions.question: What is the main focus of Lecture 8?
choices: Supervised regression diagnostics only
Database storage and indexing
The underlying theory of nonlinear dimensionality-reduction methods
Image labelling with no dimensionality reduction
questions.explanation: The lecture introduces theory and intuition for several nonlinear dimensionality-reduction techniques.

questions.question: What does it mean for a manifold to be locally Euclidean?
choices: The entire manifold must be globally flat
A sufficiently small neighbourhood around a point behaves like a flat Euclidean space
Every point must have the same coordinates
The manifold must contain only straight lines
questions.explanation: A nonlinear manifold may be curved globally while looking flat in a small enough neighbourhood.

questions.question: Which statement about the global shape of a manifold is TRUE?
choices: It may be nonlinear even though each small neighbourhood is approximately Euclidean
It must be a single straight line
It must have zero curvature everywhere
It cannot be embedded in another space
questions.explanation: Local flatness does not require the full manifold to be globally flat.

questions.question: What continuity assumption is made about data points on a manifold?
choices: Every pair of points has identical coordinates
Only points with class labels can be connected
All connections must cross at right angles
The points can be connected in a continuous way
questions.explanation: The manifold model assumes a continuous underlying space connecting the observations.

questions.question: What is the goal when choosing low-dimensional points for a manifold embedding?
choices: Maximise the number of dimensions
Discard every local relationship
Optimally preserve a chosen property of the original high-dimensional points
Make all points equally distant
questions.explanation: A low-dimensional embedding is judged by how well it preserves a selected property of the original data.

questions.question: Which property is most commonly used to evaluate a manifold embedding in the lecture?
choices: The alphabetical order of feature names
Pairwise distances between points
The number of source files
The colour used to draw each point
questions.explanation: Pairwise distances are a common basis for comparing the geometry before and after embedding.

questions.question: If two points are close in the high-dimensional space, what should a distance-preserving manifold embedding do?
choices: Place them close together in the low-dimensional space
Force them into different components
Place them at the maximum possible distance
Remove one of the points
questions.explanation: Nearby high-dimensional observations should remain neighbours in the embedding.

questions.question: How do global manifold methods treat pairwise distances?
choices: They ignore every non-neighbour distance by definition
They use only distances to the origin
They replace distances with class labels
They treat all pairwise distances as important
questions.explanation: Global methods try to fit both near and far pairwise relationships in the low-dimensional representation.

questions.question: What should happen to points that are far apart under a global distance-preserving method?
choices: They must be merged into one point
They should become nearest neighbours
They should remain far apart in the low-dimensional embedding
Their distance should be set to zero
questions.explanation: Global methods attempt to preserve far as well as near relationships.

questions.question: What key assumption is made by local manifold methods?
choices: All long-range distances must be preserved exactly
Only local distances in the high-dimensional space are considered reliably meaningful
The manifold is globally flat
Every point belongs to a known class
questions.explanation: Local methods prioritise trustworthy neighbourhood relationships instead of trying to preserve every distance.

questions.question: Why may two distant high-dimensional points appear closer after a local manifold embedding?
choices: The method focuses on neighbourhoods and the manifold is only an approximation
The method explicitly sets every distance to zero
The input data has been duplicated
Local methods preserve all long-range distances exactly
questions.explanation: Long-range relationships can be distorted when the optimisation concentrates on preserving local structure.

questions.question: What information are local manifold methods primarily trying to preserve?
choices: Only global means
The original feature names
The order in which rows were read
Neighbourhood information
questions.explanation: Local methods model the relationships among nearby observations.

questions.question: Which scenario best suits a local manifold objective?
choices: Requiring every pairwise distance to match exactly
Ignoring all nearby relationships
Preserving which observations are immediate neighbours while allowing long-range distortion
Mapping every observation to the same location
questions.explanation: A local objective protects small-scale neighbourhood structure rather than the complete global geometry.

questions.question: How can a principal component be interpreted geometrically?
choices: As a discrete hexagonal map only
As a linear manifold approximating high-dimensional data
As a graph cut with no projection
As a class label predicted by regression
questions.explanation: A principal component gives a straight low-dimensional direction through the data.

questions.question: What quantity is minimised when fitting the principal-component line described in the lecture?
choices: The total squared distance from points to their orthogonal projections on the line
Only the vertical response error
The number of graph vertices
The count of non-zero class labels
questions.explanation: PCA fits a line by minimising orthogonal least-squares reconstruction error.

questions.question: What mapping was produced when the first two principal components were retained from p-dimensional data?
choices: A mapping from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to no dimensions
A mapping from class labels to file names
A mapping from a graph to a single edge
A mapping from $\mathbb{R}^p$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$
questions.explanation: Two retained components provide a two-dimensional coordinate for each p-dimensional observation.

questions.question: How do principal curves generalise principal components?
choices: They require the data to be globally flat
They remove every distance calculation
They replace the straight approximating line with a smooth curve
They force all points onto a rectangular grid
questions.explanation: Principal curves extend the linear principal-component idea to a nonlinear one-dimensional manifold.

questions.question: How is a principal surface obtained conceptually from a principal curve?
choices: Replace the curve with a class label
Extend the curve idea to a higher-dimensional continuous surface
Use no parameters at all
Restrict the representation to one isolated point
questions.explanation: A principal surface uses more than one manifold coordinate to model a continuous higher-dimensional surface.

questions.question: What common objective links principal components, principal curves and principal surfaces?
choices: Estimate a continuous low-dimensional manifold representation of the data
Create a supervised classifier
Maximise the number of original features
Make all observations independent
questions.explanation: All three approximate data using a lower-dimensional geometric object, differing mainly in its flexibility.

questions.question: What is the main geometric objective of a principal curve $f(\lambda)$?
choices: Pass through only the most extreme outlier
Maximise every point-to-curve distance
Create disconnected graph components
Pass through the middle of the data while minimising point-to-curve distances
questions.explanation: A principal curve is fitted as a smooth central path through the observations.

questions.question: How is $f(\lambda)$ described mathematically?
choices: A scalar class label with no coordinates
A square adjacency matrix
A smooth parameterised vector curve in $\mathbb{R}^p$
A list of unrelated feature names
questions.explanation: The curve returns a p-coordinate point for each value of its parameter.

questions.question: How many coordinate functions does a principal curve in $\mathbb{R}^p$ contain?
choices: Exactly one coordinate regardless of p
p coordinate functions
N squared coordinate functions
No coordinate functions
questions.explanation: The vector-valued curve has one coordinate function for each of the p input dimensions.

questions.question: What does the parameter $\lambda$ usually represent for a principal curve?
choices: Position along the curve, usually measured by arc length
The number of class labels
The graph degree matrix
The learning rate of a neural network
questions.explanation: The parameter indexes location along the fitted curve and is commonly interpreted as arc length.

questions.question: Why is smoothing applied between computed values of a principal curve?
choices: The curve must be converted into class labels
Smoothing creates more input dimensions
The graph Laplacian cannot contain decimals
The parameter values are discrete, but the desired manifold is continuous
questions.explanation: Smoothing connects discrete fitted curve points into a continuous path.

questions.question: What self-consistency property does a principal curve satisfy?
choices: Every curve point equals the most distant observation
The curve contains only observations with zero variance
Each point on the curve is the average of data points that project to it
Every projection is chosen randomly
questions.explanation: The fitted curve passes through the conditional mean of the observations assigned to each curve location.

questions.question: What does $\lambda_f(x)$ identify for a data point x?
choices: The class label of x
The closest point or parameter location on the current curve
The largest eigenvalue of x
The degree of a graph vertex
questions.explanation: The projection index associates each observation with its nearest location on the curve.

questions.question: What does $f(\lambda)=E(X\mid\lambda_f(X)=\lambda)$ express?
choices: The curve point is the mean of observations projected to that location
The curve point is the farthest observation
Every observation has the same projection
The curve is an adjacency matrix
questions.explanation: This conditional-expectation equation states the self-consistency condition for a principal curve.

questions.question: What happens in the curve-update step of the principal-curve algorithm?
choices: All coordinates are discarded
Only the response variable is minimised
The similarity graph is made fully disconnected
Each coordinate function is replaced by the average of observations assigned to each curve location
questions.explanation: The expectation step smooths or averages the observations associated with each part of the curve.

questions.question: What happens in the projection step of the principal-curve algorithm?
choices: The input data is replaced by random weights
The number of variables is doubled
The curve is fixed and each data point is assigned to its closest curve location
The response variable is predicted from one feature
questions.explanation: The projection step minimises the squared distance between each observation and the current curve.

questions.question: When does the iterative principal-curve procedure stop?
choices: After exactly one observation
When the chosen convergence change falls below a threshold
Only when every distance becomes infinite
When all class labels are removed
questions.explanation: The update and projection steps repeat until the improvement or change is sufficiently small.

questions.question: How does the parameterisation of a principal surface differ from that of a principal curve?
choices: A principal surface can use two manifold parameters instead of one
A principal surface has no coordinates
A principal curve always uses more parameters than a surface
A surface requires a class label as its only parameter
questions.explanation: Two parameters allow the mapping to sweep out a two-dimensional surface rather than a one-dimensional curve.

questions.question: Why can a principal surface represent half-sphere data better than ordinary PCA?
choices: It forces the data onto a single straight line
It removes all local distances
It requires the classes to have identical coordinates
It can bend to follow the curved two-dimensional structure
questions.explanation: A curved surface can follow the nonlinear geometry, while a flat PCA plane is only a linear approximation.

questions.question: What error does ordinary regression minimise in the comparison shown in the lecture?
choices: Orthogonal deviations in every variable
The number of graph edges
Deviations in the response variable
The distance between SOM nodes only
questions.explanation: Regression treats one variable as the response and minimises errors measured in that response direction.

questions.question: What error does a principal component or principal curve minimise?
choices: Only errors in a chosen response variable
Deviations involving all variables through projection distance
Only the class-label error
Only the number of observations
questions.explanation: Principal methods are symmetric across variables and minimise reconstruction or projection distances.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of principal curves?
choices: They provide a smooth, continuous manifold approximation
They require a universally fixed definition
They cannot process large datasets
They are immune to parameter choices
questions.explanation: Smoothness and continuity let the curve model a nonlinear path through the data.

questions.question: What does it mean that principal curves use non-parametric coordinate functions?
choices: The curve contains no coordinates
The method requires labelled classes
The output must be a rectangular grid
The curve shape is learned flexibly from the data rather than fixed to a predetermined form
questions.explanation: Non-parametric functions allow the data to determine the fitted curve shape.

questions.question: Why can principal curves be used on large datasets according to the lecture?
choices: They never calculate a distance
They use only one observation
Their minimisation procedure is computationally efficient
They replace the dataset with a constant
questions.explanation: The lecture lists computationally efficient minimisation as an advantage.

questions.question: What can heavily affect the result of a principal-curve analysis?
choices: The spelling of the file name only
The choice of algorithm parameters
The colour of the plotted points only
The order of answer choices
questions.explanation: The fitted manifold can change substantially when smoothing and other parameters change.

questions.question: Which theoretical limitation of principal curves is identified in the lecture?
choices: There is no single universally agreed mathematical definition
They cannot represent a curve
They are always supervised
They require a graph with no edges
questions.explanation: Different formulations exist, so the exact definition is not completely universal.

questions.question: Why are principal curves prone to overfitting?
choices: They always use too few parameters
They discard all nonlinear structure
They prohibit smoothing
The observed data directly defines the fitted curve
questions.explanation: A flexible curve can follow noise or sample-specific irregularities when it is learned directly from the data.

questions.question: What does the spectrum refer to in a spectral method?
choices: The colours used in a plot
The list of class names
The eigenvalues of the system or matrix being analysed
The order of input rows
questions.explanation: Spectral methods use eigenvalues and their eigenvectors to reveal structure.

questions.question: How does spectral clustering generalise a method such as k-means?
choices: It requires all clusters to be spherical
It can reveal cluster structures beyond simple spherical or elliptical groups
It removes the need for any similarity measure
It assigns clusters from feature names
questions.explanation: The spectral embedding can make complex cluster geometry separable before a simple clustering step.

questions.question: What is the broad sequence used by spectral clustering?
choices: Build a similarity matrix, find its spectral representation, then cluster the eigenvector coordinates
Run regression, remove the response, then sort file names
Choose random labels, calculate a mean, then duplicate points
Create a SOM grid, delete its weights, then fit PCA
questions.explanation: Spectral clustering converts pairwise similarities into eigenvector features and clusters those features.

questions.question: What are the dimensions of the similarity matrix for N data points?
choices: $p \times 1$ regardless of N
$2 \times 2$ for every dataset
$N \times 0$
$N \times N$
questions.explanation: The matrix contains one pairwise similarity entry for each ordered pair of N observations.

questions.question: What restriction is placed on pairwise similarities $s_{ij}$?
choices: They must all be negative
They must all equal one
They are non-negative
They must be class labels
questions.explanation: The lecture defines the similarity weights as values greater than or equal to zero.

questions.question: Which expression represents the radial-basis similarity used in the lecture?
choices: $s_{ij}=x_i+x_j+c$
$s_{ij}=\exp(-\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2/c)$
$s_{ij}=\lVert x_i\rVert/0$
$s_{ij}=c-\exp(x_i)$
questions.explanation: The RBF similarity decreases exponentially as squared distance grows.

questions.question: What role does the positive parameter c play in the RBF similarity?
choices: It scales how quickly similarity decreases with distance
It gives the number of input rows
It is the class label
It forces every similarity to zero
questions.explanation: Changing c changes the locality or width of the similarity function.

questions.question: How many vertices does the similarity graph have for N observations?
choices: Exactly two vertices
One vertex for each feature name only
No vertices
N vertices, one for each observation
questions.explanation: Each data point becomes one vertex in the graph.

questions.question: Under the threshold rule, when are two vertices connected?
choices: When their similarity is negative
Only when they are the same observation
When their similarity is greater than a chosen threshold $\epsilon$
When their feature names match
questions.explanation: Thresholding keeps edges only for pairs considered sufficiently similar.

questions.question: What does the adjacency matrix W store?
choices: The original class labels only
The edge weights between connected data points
The names of all features
The principal-curve parameters
questions.explanation: W is the matrix representation of weighted connections in the similarity graph.

questions.question: What is stored on the diagonal of the degree matrix G?
choices: The sum of edge weights connected to each vertex
The class label of each vertex
The smallest feature value
The number of source documents
questions.explanation: Each degree value measures the total connection weight of its vertex.

questions.question: How is the unnormalised graph Laplacian defined?
choices: $L=G+W$
$L=W/G$
$L=G-W$
questions.explanation: Subtracting the adjacency matrix from the degree matrix produces the unnormalised Laplacian.

questions.question: Which expression is given as an example of a normalised graph Laplacian?
choices: $L=I+G+W$
questions.explanation: The normalised form adjusts adjacency weights by node degree.

questions.question: What does the graph Laplacian provide?
choices: A list of response-variable errors
A matrix representation of the similarity graph
A rectangular SOM grid only
A replacement for all input observations
questions.explanation: The Laplacian encodes the graph structure in a form suitable for spectral analysis.

questions.question: How does the Laplacian reformulate the original clustering task?
choices: As a graph-partitioning problem
As a supervised regression problem
As a file-sorting problem
As a random feature-deletion problem
questions.explanation: Clusters become connected graph regions separated by weak or absent connections.

questions.question: What do clusters represent in the similarity graph?
choices: Random collections of feature names
Only vertices with zero degree
Response variables with identical spelling
Connected or strongly connected local neighbourhoods
questions.explanation: A cluster corresponds to a graph region whose vertices are connected more strongly to one another than to other regions.

questions.question: Why is the graph Laplacian useful when an exact graph cut is difficult?
choices: It guarantees the exact cut without computation
It deletes all graph edges
It provides a spectral approximation to an NP-hard partitioning problem
It converts the graph into labels directly
questions.explanation: The continuous spectral formulation makes it possible to approximate a hard discrete graph-cut problem.

questions.question: What does mutual k-nearest-neighbour graph construction require?
choices: Only one point must know the other exists
Each of two connected points must be among the other point's nearest neighbours
Every point must connect to every other point
All points must have identical coordinates
questions.explanation: Mutual neighbourhoods create a more selective local graph than one-way nearest-neighbour links.

questions.question: What happens to $w_{ij}$ when two points are not mutual nearest neighbours under the stated rule?
choices: It is set to zero
It is set to infinity
It becomes a class label
It is replaced by the mean target value
questions.explanation: Non-neighbour pairs are disconnected in the local adjacency matrix.

questions.question: How can repeated choices of the RBF parameter c be used?
choices: To change the number of observations
To create response labels
To remove the adjacency matrix
To control how local or broad the similarity behaviour is
questions.explanation: Different scale values change which distances produce meaningful similarities.

questions.question: What does the number of zero eigenvalues of a graph Laplacian indicate?
choices: The number of original features
The number of response variables
The number of connected components in the graph
The number of SOM iterations
questions.explanation: Each disconnected connected component contributes a zero eigenvalue.

questions.question: What is always true about the smallest eigenvalue of a graph Laplacian?
choices: It is always negative
There is at least one eigenvalue equal to zero
It always equals the number of features
It is always greater than one
questions.explanation: Even a fully connected graph has the trivial zero eigenvalue.

questions.question: What would it mean if every Laplacian eigenvalue were zero?
choices: Every vertex is disconnected from every other vertex
The graph is one dense connected component
All edge weights are infinite
The graph has only one observation
questions.explanation: A graph with no edges consists of isolated connected components, yielding zero eigenvalues throughout.

questions.question: What does a Laplacian eigenvalue close to zero indicate?
choices: A very strong connection
A missing input feature
A supervised class boundary
A weak connection between parts of the graph
questions.explanation: Small non-zero eigenvalues correspond to graph regions joined only weakly.

questions.question: What does a large Laplacian eigenvalue indicate in the lecture?
choices: A fully disconnected component
No similarity information
Strongly connected structure
A failed file load
questions.explanation: Large eigenvalues are associated with strong internal graph connections or finer connected structure.

questions.question: What is the spectral gap as defined on the Laplacian eigenvalue slide?
choices: The largest class label
The first non-zero eigenvalue
The difference between input dimensions
The final SOM learning rate
questions.explanation: The first non-zero eigenvalue reflects how densely the graph is connected.

questions.question: What information does the Fiedler value provide?
choices: The minimum cut that divides the graph into two connected components
The average response error
The number of original features
The final principal-curve parameter
questions.explanation: The second eigenvalue identifies the weakest division that can split a connected graph into two parts.

questions.question: Which eigenvectors are used to form a Laplacian Eigenmap embedding?
choices: Only the eigenvector with the largest negative eigenvalue
Randomly selected feature columns
Only vectors of class labels
Those associated with the first m relevant eigenvalues after excluding the trivial zero eigenvalue
questions.explanation: The low-frequency non-trivial Laplacian eigenvectors provide the embedding coordinates.

questions.question: In the embedding matrix Z, what does each row represent?
choices: One source document
One class name
One original data point
One graph-cut algorithm
questions.explanation: The row for $x_i$ contains that observation's coordinates in the selected eigenvector space.

questions.question: In the embedding matrix Z, what does each column represent?
choices: One original file name
One selected Laplacian eigenvector
One response-variable error
One SOM neighbourhood radius only
questions.explanation: Each chosen eigenvector supplies one coordinate dimension of the spectral embedding.

questions.question: How should the number m of Laplacian eigenvectors be chosen?
choices: Inspect the eigenvalues for a large spectral gap
Always choose every eigenvector
Always choose exactly one
Use the alphabetic order of the features
questions.explanation: A pronounced eigenvalue gap suggests a natural number of meaningful embedding dimensions or clusters.

questions.question: What can be done with the resulting low-dimensional eigenmap coordinates?
choices: Use them only as file names
Discard them immediately
Convert them back into identical high-dimensional points
Plot them or provide them to another learning algorithm
questions.explanation: The eigenvectors form useful reduced features for visualisation or downstream modelling.

questions.question: What did each row of the MNIST input matrix represent?
choices: One class label only
One graph edge
Pixel intensities for one handwritten-digit image
One SOM learning rate
questions.explanation: Each image was flattened into a high-dimensional vector of pixel intensities.

questions.question: What was used as the two-dimensional coordinate for each MNIST image?
choices: Its file name and row number
Its values in the two leading selected eigenvectors
Its maximum and minimum class label
Two random pixel positions
questions.explanation: Two spectral eigenvector components give each image a point in the plotted embedding.

questions.question: What can the first large gap in the ordered eigenvalues indicate?
choices: A plausible number of clusters
The number of input files
The exact learning rate
The number of response variables
questions.explanation: A large separation after the first few eigenvalues suggests that those earlier modes represent the main connected groups.

questions.question: If there is a large gap between the fourth and fifth eigenvalues, what cluster count does the lecture suggest?
choices: Five hundred clusters
One cluster regardless of the graph
No clusters
Four clusters
questions.explanation: The slide interprets the first large gap after the fourth eigenvalue as evidence for four connected groups.

questions.question: How does spectral clustering go beyond Laplacian Eigenmaps?
choices: It removes all eigenvectors
It replaces similarities with response errors
It clusters the rows of the spectral embedding with k-means
It requires the original clusters to be spherical
questions.explanation: After producing eigenvector coordinates, spectral clustering applies a clustering method to those new features.

questions.question: What feature vector is clustered for data point $x_i$ in spectral clustering?
choices: Its original file path
The row containing its components across the selected eigenvectors
Its response label only
The diagonal of the degree matrix only
questions.explanation: Each row of Z describes one observation in spectral space and is the input to k-means.

questions.question: Why can spectral clustering be relatively insensitive to outliers?
choices: It preserves local neighbourhood structure
It deletes every point far from the mean
It forces every graph to be fully connected
It uses only response labels
questions.explanation: The similarity graph emphasises local relationships, limiting the influence of isolated distant points.

questions.question: What does stability with respect to embedding mean in this context?
choices: The method always returns the same random seed
The input coordinates never change
Every cluster has identical size
The method aims to recover the same underlying manifold structure
questions.explanation: Spectral coordinates are derived from the same graph geometry rather than an arbitrary visual projection.

questions.question: Which design choice must be made before spectral clustering?
choices: Whether to remove all observations
How to name the source file
How to construct the similarity graph
Whether to use any numerical values
questions.explanation: A fully connected, thresholded or nearest-neighbour graph can lead to different results.

questions.question: Which set contains hyperparameters mentioned for spectral clustering?
choices: Only the spelling of feature names
Neighbour count k and the RBF scale c
Only the page number
Only the response-variable name
questions.explanation: Neighbourhood and similarity-scale choices control the graph and therefore the embedding.

questions.question: What is a limitation when a new data point arrives after spectral clustering?
choices: The spectral procedure generally has to be repeated to include it
The point is always mapped without computation
The point automatically receives the largest eigenvalue
The graph cannot contain new vertices
questions.explanation: The basic method does not directly provide the same simple out-of-sample mapping as some parametric transformations.

questions.question: Which eigenvector-related decision can be unclear in spectral clustering?
choices: Whether eigenvectors contain letters
Whether every eigenvector is a class name
Whether eigenvectors should be deleted before use
How many eigenvectors to extract and whether they can be computed efficiently
questions.explanation: The correct embedding dimension and computational feasibility may both be uncertain.

questions.question: Which Laplacian choice may require judgement?
choices: Whether to use a negative number of observations
Whether to remove the similarity matrix
Whether to use a normalised or unnormalised Laplacian
Whether to use no graph vertices
questions.explanation: Different Laplacian normalisations encode graph structure differently and can change results.

questions.question: Why is the concentric-circles example difficult for ordinary k-means in the original space?
choices: The data has no numerical coordinates
The clusters are non-convex rings rather than spherical groups around centroids
Every point is identical
There is only one observation
questions.explanation: Centroid-based Euclidean partitions do not naturally separate nested rings.

questions.question: Which eigenvectors are plotted in the toy spectral-clustering example?
choices: Those corresponding to the smallest non-zero eigenvalues
Only those with negative infinite eigenvalues
Random feature columns
Only the trivial zero eigenvector
questions.explanation: The non-trivial low-frequency eigenvectors reveal the large-scale connected groups.

questions.question: What final step produced clear class separation in the concentric-circles example?
choices: Regression on the original y-coordinate
Random deletion of graph edges
Sorting points by file name
K-means clustering of the rows of the selected eigenvectors
questions.explanation: The spectral transformation makes the ring structure separable in the eigenvector coordinate space.

questions.question: How are self-organising maps related to k-means?
choices: They are supervised regression models
They contain no distance calculations
They are a constrained form of k-means with a topology-preserving output map
They always produce a continuous curve
questions.explanation: SOMs add neighbourhood and map-topology constraints to competitive prototype learning.

questions.question: What is the usual dimensionality of a SOM output space?
choices: The same p dimensions as the input in every case
Two dimensions
Zero dimensions
Exactly one hundred dimensions
questions.explanation: SOMs commonly map high-dimensional observations onto a two-dimensional lattice for interpretation and visualisation.

questions.question: What property does a SOM try to preserve in its output map?
choices: Topological neighbourhood structure, usually based on Euclidean distance
The exact original feature names
Only the response-variable error
A fully disconnected graph
questions.explanation: Nearby or similar inputs should map to nearby nodes on the organised grid.

questions.question: How do SOMs differ from principal curves and surfaces?
choices: SOMs cannot reduce dimensionality
Principal curves use only class labels
SOMs require a response variable
SOMs use a discrete lattice instead of a continuous manifold
questions.explanation: Both seek a lower-dimensional organisation, but SOM output positions are discrete grid nodes.

questions.question: In what sense is a SOM an artificial neural network?
choices: It must be trained with backpropagation
It contains only response labels
Its map nodes act as neurons with adaptable weight vectors
It has no parameters to update
questions.explanation: The nodes are neuron-like prototypes positioned in input space by learned weight vectors.

questions.question: What learning style is used to train a SOM?
choices: Supervised error-correction learning only
Competitive learning
Ordinary least-squares regression
Random graph cutting
questions.explanation: Nodes compete to be the closest prototype to each input instead of learning from a labelled target error.

questions.question: Which node wins when an input is presented to a SOM?
choices: The node whose weight vector is closest to the input
The node with the longest name
The node farthest from the input
A node chosen from the class label
questions.explanation: The best matching unit is selected using a distance measure such as Euclidean distance.

questions.question: Which weights are adjusted after a SOM selects a winning node?
choices: Only the most distant node
Every input feature name
No weights are adjusted
The winner and its map neighbours
questions.explanation: Updating a neighbourhood around the winner is what preserves map topology.

questions.question: Which shapes are commonly used to initialise a SOM map?
choices: Only a continuous sphere
Only a single straight regression line
Rectangular or hexagonal grids
A graph with no vertices
questions.explanation: The discrete map is usually arranged as a rectangular or hexagonal lattice.

questions.question: What does each SOM node weight vector represent?
choices: A class label that never changes
A position in the original input-data space
The number of iterations completed
The page number of the lecture
questions.explanation: Node weights are prototypes in the p-dimensional input space.

questions.question: What does it mean to bend the SOM grid during training?
choices: Iteratively move node prototypes so the grid follows the structure of the input data
Add more original features at every step
Make all node weights identical
Remove neighbourhood relationships
questions.explanation: Training adapts the grid in input space while retaining neighbourhood relationships in map space.

questions.question: What must be chosen before SOM training begins?
choices: The final class label of every point
A graph cut with no data
The exact winning node for every future input
The map size and whether its grid is rectangular or hexagonal
questions.explanation: Map dimensions and topology are core configuration choices.

questions.question: How are SOM weight vectors initially set in the stated algorithm?
choices: They are all fixed permanently at zero
They are copied from class labels
They are assigned random initial values
They are removed before training
questions.explanation: Training begins from initial prototype weights that are then adapted.

questions.question: What happens after an input vector is sampled during SOM training?
choices: It is immediately deleted
Its distance to every node weight is computed to find the closest node
It becomes the learning rate
Its feature names are alphabetised
questions.explanation: The best matching unit is the node minimising the chosen input-space distance.
