questions.question: What does the neighbourhood function h control in a SOM update?
choices: How strongly nodes are updated according to their map distance from the winner
The number of source files
The response-variable error
The original feature names
questions.explanation: Nodes nearer the winning location receive a larger update than distant nodes.

questions.question: What happens if the SOM neighbourhood is reduced so that only the winner is updated?
choices: The map becomes a principal surface
The graph becomes fully disconnected by definition
The method becomes supervised regression
The method essentially reverts to k-means
questions.explanation: Without neighbour updates, prototype competition behaves like centroid updates in k-means.

questions.question: How should the SOM learning rate $\alpha$ change during training?
choices: It must increase without limit
It must always equal the number of features
It should decrease over iterations
It should be replaced by a class label
questions.explanation: A decaying learning rate allows large early adjustments and smaller refinements later.

questions.question: When does SOM training stop?
choices: Immediately after initialising weights
At convergence or after the maximum number of iterations
Only when every input is identical
When the output becomes continuous
questions.explanation: The iterative update runs until a stability or iteration stopping condition is reached.

questions.question: What is distinctive about the two-dimensional SOM output space?
choices: It takes only discrete node locations
It contains every possible continuous coordinate
It always has the same dimension as the input
It contains no representation of new inputs
questions.explanation: A SOM maps observations to positions on a finite lattice rather than an arbitrary continuous plane.

questions.question: How is a new observation mapped after the SOM has been trained?
choices: The entire SOM must be deleted
It is assigned randomly
It is placed at the largest eigenvalue
It is assigned to the node with the closest learned weight vector
questions.explanation: The learned prototypes define an out-of-sample mapping through nearest-node assignment.

questions.question: What is the first of the four SOM process components summarised in the lecture?
choices: Delete losing nodes
Choose a response variable
Initialise the map weights
Compute a graph cut
questions.explanation: The process begins by assigning starting weight vectors to map nodes.

questions.question: What determines the neighbourhood updated for a particular input?
choices: The input file name
The location of the winning node in map space
The number of class labels
The page on which the method is described
questions.explanation: Nearby nodes on the map are updated because the winner defines the local output neighbourhood.

questions.question: How are nodes far from the winner treated in the lecture's four-part summary?
choices: Their weights are lowered or left less likely to match similar inputs
They receive the largest positive update
They become class labels
They replace the winning node
questions.explanation: The competitive update favours the winner and its neighbours over distant losing nodes.

questions.question: Which set lists advantages of SOMs given in the lecture?
choices: Supervised only, no visual output and slow training
No parameters, no data requirements and exact mappings
Guaranteed perfect clustering and zero reconstruction error
Unsupervised, interpretable visualisations, scalable to large data and generally fast training
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights unsupervised learning, visual interpretability, scalability and speed as advantages.

questions.question: Why should SOM and k-means reconstruction errors sometimes be compared?
choices: K-means contains no centroids
SOMs cannot calculate distances
The topology constraint imposed by the SOM may not be appropriate for the data
Reconstruction error is always zero
questions.explanation: The added map constraint can worsen representation, so empirical comparison can show whether it is justified.

questions.question: Which SOM settings are identified as parameters that must be chosen?
choices: Only the source-file name
Learning rate, neighbourhood-distance threshold and number of iterations
Only the class-label spelling
Only the graph Laplacian normalisation
questions.explanation: SOM behaviour depends on several training and neighbourhood hyperparameters.

questions.question: What mapping problem can occur with SOMs?
choices: Clusters may be divided too many times and a perfect mapping may be difficult to find
Every cluster is guaranteed to remain intact
The method always returns one node
All observations become identical
questions.explanation: The discrete topology may split natural groups or fail to represent them perfectly.

questions.question: How can SOMs support document organisation and retrieval?
choices: Use raw text without any encoding
Sort documents only by file size
Replace every document with the same vector
Map vectorised documents so clusters of terms and representative words can be identified
questions.explanation: After text is encoded numerically, nearby map regions can reveal recurring term patterns and document groups.

questions.question: Which SOM use case treats unusual observations as important?
choices: Ordinary response-variable regression only
Graph normalisation only
Fraud or outlier detection
Feature-name sorting
questions.explanation: Inputs that map unusually or far from established map regions can signal anomalous behaviour.

questions.question: Which image-processing use case is listed for SOMs?
choices: Increasing every image to infinite dimensions
Colour quantisation
Removing all pixel values
Assigning random captions
questions.explanation: Colour quantisation uses a limited set of representative colours learned from image pixels.

questions.question: Which pair contains additional SOM applications listed in the lecture?
choices: Clustering and visualisation
Supervised language translation and database joins
Only linear regression and hypothesis testing
Graph deletion and file compression only
questions.explanation: SOMs are widely used for exploratory clustering and low-dimensional visualisation.

questions.question: Which method produces a discrete topology-preserving lattice rather than a continuous curve or eigenvector embedding?
choices: A principal curve
A Laplacian Eigenmap
Ordinary PCA
A self-organising map
questions.explanation: SOMs represent the output as nodes on a discrete grid; the other methods use continuous curves, linear projections or spectral coordinates.

questions.question: Which pair of methods both begin from local similarity structure encoded by a graph Laplacian?
choices: PCA and linear regression
Principal curves and ordinary k-means only
Laplacian Eigenmaps and spectral clustering
Factor Analysis and ICA
questions.explanation: Both methods use Laplacian eigenvectors; spectral clustering adds clustering of the resulting row coordinates.

questions.question: Why does the graph drawn in the worked example suggest two natural clusters?
choices: It contains two densely connected groups joined by a relatively weak bridge
Every vertex is disconnected
All vertices occupy the same position
The graph has no internal edges
questions.explanation: The drawing contains two tightly connected groups with only a limited connection between them, which is the structure spectral methods seek to expose.

questions.question: What feature of the Laplacian spectrum would reflect the weak bridge between the two groups in the worked example?
choices: A small non-zero eigenvalue after the trivial zero eigenvalue
No zero eigenvalue at all
Only negative infinite eigenvalues
An eigenvalue equal to the number of input features by definition
questions.explanation: A weak connection between otherwise cohesive graph regions produces a small non-zero Laplacian eigenvalue.

questions.question: If the single bridge between the two dense groups were removed, what would happen to the number of zero Laplacian eigenvalues?
choices: It would indicate two connected components
It would indicate that every vertex is still in one component
It would become negative
It would no longer be related to graph connectivity
questions.explanation: Removing the bridge separates the graph into two connected components, and the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue equals the number of connected components.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of t-SNE?
choices: Visualising nonlinear high-dimensional data in two or three dimensions
Maximising the variance retained in every original feature
Training a reusable classifier for unseen observations
Replacing all clustering algorithms with a deterministic method
questions.explanation: The lecture presents t-SNE as a two- or three-dimensional visualisation method for nonlinear high-dimensional data.

questions.question: Compared with PCA, which pairwise relationships does t-SNE primarily preserve?
choices: Only the largest pairwise distances
All pairwise distances exactly
Only distances between cluster centroids
Small pairwise distances or local similarities
questions.explanation: t-SNE focuses on nearby observations, whereas PCA preserves large pairwise distances as part of maximising variance.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts PCA and t-SNE?
choices: PCA is iterative, while t-SNE has a closed-form map for new points
PCA preserves only class labels, while t-SNE preserves only feature names
PCA emphasises large pairwise distances, while t-SNE emphasises local similarities
PCA is nonlinear, while t-SNE is strictly linear
questions.explanation: The stated contrast is between PCA preserving large-scale variance and t-SNE preserving small, local relationships.

questions.question: What does t-SNE compare during optimisation?
choices: The number of features with the number of clusters
Pairwise similarities in the high-dimensional and low-dimensional spaces
Only the marginal mean of each feature
The class accuracy before and after projection
questions.explanation: t-SNE defines similarities in both spaces and optimises the low-dimensional arrangement so that they agree.

questions.question: Which structure is t-SNE designed to preserve most strongly?
choices: Local neighbourhood structure
Exact global geometry
The original coordinate axes
The ordering of feature columns
questions.explanation: t-SNE is a manifold-learning method that focuses on local rather than global structure.

questions.question: What can be inferred reliably from points lying close together within a t-SNE cluster?
choices: The cluster is exactly twice as important as a smaller cluster
The cluster centre is the global mean of the original data
The points must have identical original feature values
The points are highly related under the high-dimensional similarity measure
questions.explanation: Nearby points within a t-SNE cluster represent locally similar observations, not necessarily identical observations.

questions.question: Which interpretation of distances between separate t-SNE clusters is appropriate?
choices: They always equal the difference between class means
They are meaningful only when the clusters have equal sizes
They do not provide a reliable measure of similarity between the clusters
They are exact Euclidean distances from the original space
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly warns that between-cluster distances are not an actual indication of cluster similarity.

questions.question: Why can a fitted t-SNE map not normally be reused directly for new data?
choices: Every new observation must already have a class label
Adding new data requires rebuilding the entire iterative map
t-SNE deletes the original observations after fitting
The method accepts categorical values only once
questions.explanation: t-SNE is iterative and does not provide the reusable transformation described for methods such as PCA.

questions.question: For which task does the lecture recommend t-SNE most strongly?
choices: Visualisation
Learning a general-purpose reusable embedding
Forecasting a time series
Estimating missing values
questions.explanation: The lecture recommends t-SNE for visualisation and urges care if it is treated as a learned embedding.

questions.question: Why can two t-SNE runs on the same data produce different layouts?
choices: The input features are automatically renamed between runs
t-SNE always changes the requested number of dimensions
The high-dimensional similarities are discarded before optimisation
The result depends strongly on parameters and initialisation, and the method is not deterministic
questions.explanation: The output is parameter-dependent and stochastic, so repeated runs need not match.

questions.question: A t-SNE plot has two clusters that are far apart. Which conclusion is NOT justified?
choices: The layout may change with another initialisation
The plot is primarily a visualisation of local structure
The original groups are separated by that same large global distance
Points close together within a cluster are locally similar
questions.explanation: The spacing of separate t-SNE clusters should not be read as faithful global distance.

questions.question: Which statement about t-SNE output is TRUE?
choices: It preserves all original distances exactly
It can show highly related points within clusters without explaining differences between separate clusters
It guarantees a globally optimal layout
It creates a deterministic projection matrix for future observations
questions.explanation: t-SNE is strong at local grouping but does not support detailed global comparisons between clusters.

questions.question: Which divergence does t-SNE minimise between high- and low-dimensional joint probabilities?
choices: Kullback-Leibler divergence
Jensen-Shannon distance only
Mean absolute feature error
The Gini impurity
questions.explanation: The algorithm minimises Kullback-Leibler divergence between the two probability distributions.

questions.question: What are the similarities between data points converted into in the t-SNE overview?
choices: Binary class labels
Principal-component loadings
Graph colours
Joint probabilities
questions.explanation: The overview describes converting similarities into joint probabilities before optimisation.

questions.question: Why may different t-SNE initialisations yield different results?
choices: It uses a fixed closed-form eigendecomposition
It always starts from the same global optimum
Its cost function is non-convex
Its cost function has no variables
questions.explanation: A non-convex objective can have different locally optimal solutions.

questions.question: What does the conditional probability p(i|j) represent in the lecture?
choices: The chance that a point receives the correct class label
How close one high-dimensional point is to another under a Gaussian centred on the conditioning point
The probability that two low-dimensional clusters have equal sizes
The variance explained by a principal component
questions.explanation: The high-dimensional conditional similarity is computed using a Gaussian neighbourhood around a point.

questions.question: Which distribution is used to model neighbourhood similarity in the original high-dimensional space?
choices: A Gaussian distribution
A uniform distribution over the whole map
A Student t-distribution with a long tail
A Poisson distribution over cluster counts
questions.explanation: The high-dimensional conditional similarities use a Gaussian kernel.

questions.question: Why does each high-dimensional point have its own sigma value?
choices: To assign every point a different output dimension
To force every point into a separate cluster
To encode its class label in the variance
To adapt the Gaussian neighbourhood width to local density
questions.explanation: Point-specific bandwidths allow t-SNE to adapt similarity calculations to different local densities.

questions.question: How does the Gaussian variance behave in denser regions?
choices: It is identical to the number of dimensions
It becomes negative
It is smaller
It is always infinite
questions.explanation: The lecture states that denser areas use a smaller variance.

questions.question: What does the t-SNE perplexity parameter set?
choices: The learning rate of a classifier trained afterward
The effective number of neighbours attracting each point
The exact number of output clusters
The number of principal components retained
questions.explanation: Perplexity controls the effective neighbourhood size used for attractive relationships.

questions.question: During t-SNE optimisation, which pairs experience a repulsive force?
choices: All pairs of points
Only pairs in the same labelled class
Only the single nearest-neighbour pair
No pairs when perplexity is below 50
questions.explanation: All pairs repel, while only a smaller set of pairs has an attractive force.

questions.question: Which pairs experience attractive force in the t-SNE description?
choices: Every possible pair equally
Only pairs from different datasets
Only the two most distant points
A relatively small number of neighbour pairs
questions.explanation: Perplexity determines a small effective neighbourhood whose pairs attract one another.

questions.question: What tends to happen when t-SNE perplexity is too small?
choices: The method becomes deterministic
The low-dimensional similarity becomes Gaussian
Repulsion dominates and the map can inflate into a poorly separated bubble-like shape
All clusters collapse to one exact coordinate
questions.explanation: Too few attractive pairs allow repulsive forces to dominate the layout.

questions.question: Why can a very small perplexity produce poor separation?
choices: The KL objective is replaced by cross-entropy
Too few pairs experience attraction
Every point is attracted to every other point
The high-dimensional variance becomes identical everywhere
questions.explanation: A very small effective neighbourhood reduces attractive constraints.

questions.question: What is a typical effect of increasing t-SNE perplexity?
choices: Clusters tend to shrink into denser structures
Clusters are guaranteed to match true labels
The embedding gains more output dimensions
The algorithm stops using pairwise similarities
questions.explanation: The lecture associates larger perplexity with denser, more compact clusters.

questions.question: What kind of information is retained more as perplexity increases?
choices: Less information about any neighbours
Only class-label information
Only the signs of feature values
More non-local information
questions.explanation: A larger effective neighbourhood incorporates relationships beyond the closest local points.

questions.question: Who chooses the perplexity value used to determine local bandwidths?
choices: The class labels in every case
The low-dimensional coordinates after optimisation
The user
The nearest-neighbour graph alone with no parameter choice
questions.explanation: Perplexity is a user-selected hyperparameter.

questions.question: Which range is suggested as a low t-SNE perplexity to explore for a good mapping?
choices: Any negative value
Approximately 5 to 50
Exactly 0 to 1
Approximately 500 to 5,000 only
questions.explanation: The lecture suggests searching for a useful low perplexity in the 5-50 range.

questions.question: Why is the same perplexity target used for all points?
choices: So that no single point has more influence merely through a larger effective neighbour count
So that every point receives the same sigma
